title: Tahun Yubileum Sebagai Hero (Hope, Efficacy, Resilience, Optimism): Sebuah Perspektif Psikospiritual
abstract: The Jubilee Year is a religious tradition that has deep meaning for Catholics, seen as a moment of grace that emphasizes liberation, forgiveness, and renewal of life. From a psychological perspective, this celebration not only functions as a spiritual ritual, but also as a coping mechanism that strengthens psychological well-being. This study aims to explore the meaning of the Jubilee Year through the HERO (Hope, Efficacy, Resilience, Optimism) framework, emphasizing how these psychospiritual dimensions are present in the experiences of the faithful. The research method used was qualitative, involving in-depth interviews with three informants who are active in spiritual communities and have undergone the Porta Sancta pilgrimage, as well as a literature review to strengthen the analysis. The data were analyzed interactively through reduction, presentation, and conclusion drawing. The results of the study show that hope is understood as spiritual energy that encourages the faithful to make peace with the past and move towards the future; self-efficacy is reflected in the belief that prayer, devotion, and concrete actions can strengthen self-confidence in the face of challenges; resilience emerges in attitudes of surrender, humility, and forgiveness that help the faithful rise from difficult experiences; while spiritual optimism is seen as the power of faith that fosters a vision of a future full of love and justice. Overall, the Jubilee Year becomes a psychospiritual space that strengthens HERO capital, making this celebration not only a liturgical tradition, but also a means of character building and resilience in facing the dynamics of life.

title: Remembering Gandhi and Rediscovering Humanity: Gandhi Jayanti 2026
abstract: Usually, the celebration of Gandhi Jayanti in India takes the form of a national observance, marked by official ceremonies in which the President, Prime Minister, and other leaders pay floral tributes and offer prayers at Gandhiji’s memorial at Raj Ghat, New Delhi. Government offices, schools, and banks remain closed. Gandhi Bhavans and other Gandhian institutions across the country organise prayer meetings and commemorative programmes. His favourite bhajans, ‘Raghupati Raghav Raja Ram’ and ‘Vaishnav Jan To’ are sung, while statues and portraits of Gandhi are garlanded.

title: Mutua Concordia: Enhancing the Responsibility of the Synod of Bishops of the Eastern Catholic Churches
abstract: Mutua concordia, an Apostolic Letter issued by Pope Leo XIV motu proprio on August 29, 2026, introduces modifications to Canons 106 and 126 of the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches (CCEO 1990). These modifications strengthen the role and responsibility of the Synod of Bishops of the Eastern Catholic Churches. It gives the Synod greater responsibility in situations where the Patriarch or Major Archbishop fails to fulfil his duties. It provides the Synod with the authority to convoke the Synod when the Patriarch or Major Archbishop fails to do so. Furthermore, when there is a serious cause, the Synod is empowered to proceed, according to the norms and procedures established in the document, toward the removal of the Patriarch or Major Archbishop from office.

title: Walking with the Courageous Suffering Servant Jesus: A Johannine Perspective
abstract: John’s powerful presentation of the passion and death of Jesus brings out not merely the suffering servant but the courageous suffering servant Jesus. After deliberating upon the violent and voluntary death of Jesus, the article highlights the unique Johannine understanding of the glorification of Jesus. That suffering is glory/glorification is a specific perspective John has emphasised in portraying the passion of Jesus. Jesus’ suffering is value-oriented and courageous suffering, which is focussed here by contemplatively going through some of the key events of the passion narrative of John.

title: A. T. Thomas
abstract: A. T. Thomas (1951-1997), a Hazaribagh Jesuit, witnesses to Jesus through his social action among the Dalits of Hazaribagh. Like Jesus, focusing on liberation, he serves the marginalised communities. His martyrdom reveals liberation (aphesis) as the heart of Christian discipleship, making visible God’s saving presence among the poor and inspiring continued commitment to justice, equality, and the transformation of society.

title: Assessing intercultural communicative competence in virtual environments: Vietnamese EFL teachers' perceptions of assessment criteria
abstract: This study examines Vietnamese tertiary EFL teachers’ perceptions of assessment-relevant abilities and behaviours for digital intercultural communication competence (DICC) in virtual environments. Drawing on a teacher-only subsample of 197 participants from universities across Vietnam, the study used a 30-item questionnaire covering five dimensions: Intercultural communication readiness, contextual sensitivity, virtual interactional competence, reflective adaptability, and operational performance. Descriptive statistics and Cronbach’s alpha were used to analyse perceived importance, response variation, and internal consistency. Findings showed stronger endorsement of respect, openness, contextual sensitivity, polite and clear language, communicative adjustment, and culturally appropriate disagreement, while confidence, participation, explicit reflection, sensitive-topic management, and broad collaboration were relatively less salient or more variable. The results suggest that teachers conceptualise assessable virtual ICC primarily as relational, context-sensitive, adaptive, and behaviorally observable competence. The study highlights the need for contextually grounded, multimethod assessment criteria in Vietnamese tertiary EFL education and offers directions for future assessment framework development.

title: UPAMANA PRAMANA IN SUSHRUTA SAMHITA NIDANA STHANA: A TAXONOMIC AND MORPHOLOGICAL STUDY
abstract: The Nidana Sthana of the Sushruta Samhita is a foundational text in Ayurvedic diagnostics that extensively utilizes Upamana Pramana (analogies and similes) to elucidate complex clinical and surgical concepts. To systematically decode this pedagogical framework, this conceptual article presents a comprehensive textual review of all 16 chapters of the Nidana Sthana, meticulously tabulating the utilized Upamanas, their specific clinical contexts, and the corresponding shloka numbers. The compilation reveals that Acharya Sushruta employed a diverse array of real-world imagery as precise diagnostic tools rather than mere poetic flourishes. The findings categorize these analogies into distinct domains: botanical and zoological imagery for soft-tissue lesions (e.g., comparing hemorrhoids to plant shoots), household physics for systemic failures (e.g., likening dropsy to oil seeping through an unbaked clay pot), and structural metaphors for anatomical deformities (e.g., mapping bone fractures to crab pinchers). Ultimately, this compilation demonstrates that bridging the gap between abstract human pathology and familiar natural phenomena provided ancient practitioners with an intuitive visual roadmap. For contemporary Ayurvedic scholars and clinicians, analyzing these ancient metaphors not only deepens the understanding of surgical pathology but also highlights a timeless pedagogical model for clinical education.

title: AN AYURVEDIC GUIDE TO THE DAILY CLOCK
abstract: If you look at a typical modern morning, it’s a masterclass in sensory overload. We jolt awake to digital alarms, immediately consume a flood of information from our screens, and rush out the door, which is physically fed, but energetically depleted. Thousands of years ago, Ayurvedic medicine proposed a radical alternative: Dinacharya(daily routine). This foundational framework for daily routine suggests that the very first choices we make upon waking don't just manage our time; they set the physiological and neurological tone for the entire day. The foundational principles outlined in Ayurveda texts, explains about how aligning daily actions with natural rhythms can effectively cut through the heavy, stagnant qualities of Kapha dosha that often manifest as morning lethargy. By contrasting modern habits with traditional practices including waking up in Brahma Muhurta, engaging in sensory cleansing, and grounding the nervous system through Abhyanga (body massage with medicated oil). These practices provides a roadmap for transforming chaotic mornings. Ultimately, it offers an accessible, scalable approach to integrate these ancient rituals, to build a sustainable foundation for lasting resilience, improved digestion, and balanced energy.

title: A major monastic centre? Rethinking Lismore’s place in the ecclesiastical landscapes of early medieval Britain
abstract: Until recent decades, the monastery of Lios Mòr (Lismore) in Argyll, Scotland, established by Saint Mo Luóc in the sixth century, was attested only via historical references and local traditions. Community-led investigations have now revealed an early medieval cemetery, sophisticated craftworking of international importance and early structures around the island’s parish church. These discoveries underscore the site’s status as a high-ranking ecclesiastical centre of the Insular north-west and elucidate its significance and integral role within the early Christian networks of Dál Riata, offering insights into the material traces of early medieval monasticism in northern Britain in the first millennium AD.

title: Carnivore scavenging patterns in terrestrial contexts: a 25-year retrospective study of forensic anthropology cases from Greece
abstract: Abstract Animal scavenging is frequently encountered in forensic investigations. The identification of scavenging is crucial, as scavengers have the potential to disrupt forensic contexts significantly by disarticulating body elements and consuming portions of bone. Determining the anatomical areas more commonly affected by scavengers can assist in recognizing the presence of scavenging activity in forensic contexts. Past forensic cases, submitted to the Forensic Anthropology Unit of the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens Medical School for analysis between 1999 and 2023, were analyzed. Of the 256 cases examined, 62 exhibited signs of carnivore scavenging, while 194 presented no such evidence. To evaluate the impact of scavenging on human decomposition, the data collected from these cases were analyzed and compared. This comparison aimed to identify and assess any statistically significant differences in preservation and environmental conditions between scavenged and non-scavenged remains. The results indicate that scavenging is more likely to occur in rural settings and areas characterized by low population density. A lower prevalence of upper limb bones was reported in cases exhibiting signs of scavenging. Furthermore, this study identified specific anatomical regions that are preferentially affected by scavenger activity. Given the relative scarcity of similar research in Europe, the present study provides valuable insights into scavenging patterns in Greece and the broader European context.

title: The Imitation of Woman's Heart 1: Data
abstract: English and Chinese editions; audio and video at Sarah Chen Memory Gate. The album that significantly altered Sarah Chen’s career is the 1988 Woman’s Heart, her first collaboration with Jonathan Lee. Promoted as Lee’s new experiment, the album is often said to have launched a new “urban woman” phase of Chen’s career1. But was Woman’s Heart a Mandopop innovation? Or was it an imitation album? Here, using a data-driven approach, we analyzed the conceptual similarity between Woman’s Heart and Chen’s 1987 English album Miracle of Love. We showed that the six Lee-written songs on Woman’s Heart were highly similar to those on Miracle of Love. The finding challenges the album's originality. Rather than a new concept album, Woman's Heart is likely a Mandopop adaptation of Chen's English work. 【女人心效颦 1. 数据】陈淑桦的职业叙事在1988年发生了转变。她和李宗盛首度合作的《女人心》在宣传上走了「制作人至上」的路线,专辑被定位为李宗盛的新尝试,他以一个全新的概念开启了陈淑桦“都市女子”的阶段1。但《女人心》真的是华语乐坛的创新吗?它会不会是一部效仿专辑?本期以数据驱动的方法,分析《女人心》和陈淑桦1987年英文专辑《爱的奇迹》(Miracle of Love)的概念相似性。 分析发现,李宗盛填词的六首歌与《爱的奇迹》在统计上有极为显著的相似性,高于陈淑桦另外43首百代歌曲中任意六首歌的六百万种组合。这个发现对《女人心》的创新性提出疑问。虽然官方宣传说《女人心》是新概念专辑,但它更可能是陈淑桦英文作品的华语效仿集。

title: Study of Robustness Index and Product Index of Dry, Adult Human Clavicle in Bangladeshi population.
abstract: The clavicle is morphologically a modified long bone of upper limb and is also an important bone for transmission of body weight from upper limb to the axial skeleton, for muscle attachment and is a significant source of bone grafting. The basic framework of human body is reflected in bones and may provide valuable information about the biological identity of the deceased which can be used for forensic anthropological perspectives. Biological sex determination is one of the most important determinations to be made from human remains and is an essential first step in the development of the biological profile in forensics, anthropology and bioarcheology. The study which was descriptive cross-sectional in nature was done among 150 (65 right and 85 left) fully ossified and dried human clavicle in Mymensingh Medical College, Bangladesh from January 2020 to December 2020. Non-random purposive sampling technique was applied for sample collection from Department of Anatomy of Mymensingh Medical College and Community Based Medical College, Bangladesh, Mymensingh. The parameters were robustness index and product index; a ratio in which the baseline data were collected by the help of flexible measuring tape and rigid osteometry board. The robustness index is the percentage ratio between the mid clavicular circumference and straight length of clavicle whereas the product index is the inverse percentage ratio of robustness index. The mean ±SD robustness index of 65 right sided clavicles were 24.94±2.66 and 85 clavicles of left side were 25.02±2.41 whereas in case of product index it became 404.86±47.28 for 65 right sided clavicles and 403.29±38.77 for 85 left sided clavicles.

title: The Despars Avicenna *Canon* Corpus: A Seven-Witness Substrate-Anchored Inventory (1431–1498)
abstract: This paper presents a substrate-anchored seven-witness inventory of Jacques Despars's commentary on Avicenna's Canon medicinae (Latin translation of Gerard of Cremona, c. 1170s), assembled inside a research substrate that tracks several hundred late medieval medical manuscripts, figures, and findings (substrate snapshot, June 2026) [Honeycutt 2025, Paduan Medical Reference dataset, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.18687530]. Despars (c. 1380–1458), regent master of medicine at the University of Paris and physician to the houses of Burgundy and France, compiled his Commentarii in Canonem between 1432 and 1453 [1][2]. The seven-witness list is anchored by Jacquart's manuscript census, the Biblissima records for the BnF witnesses, and the BSB image record for the Lyon print [1][4][5][27]. Six manuscript witnesses are catalogue-anchored; the Lyon 1498 print, BSB Munich bsb00071249 volume three, is anchored at folio imagery level and has been HTR-walked at corpus scale. A thirty-two-folio handwritten-text-recognition (HTR) walk of that print, processed under Kraken with the CATMuS Medieval 1.6.0 model, returned raw hits across seven tracked Latin pharmacological class-words (paleographer verification pending) and is reported as an Observed pattern, not as closure on the seven-witness inventory [6]. The paper situates the witnesses against Padua scholastic medicine, catalogues them with source-bounded metadata, and supplies a tier and falsification matrix.

title: The Hartlieb *Kräuterbuch* 9-Witness Corpus: A Snapshot-Bounded Census
abstract: Johannes Hartlieb's Kräuterbuch (composed ca. 1435–1450) is a German-vernacular illustrated herbal of 173 chapters, attributed in the cited standard references in the modern scholarly record to Hartlieb (Grubmüller 1981; Hayer and Schnell 2010). The work survives in nine catalogued manuscript witnesses on the current Handschriftencensus record (Werk 2317, snapshot 2026-05-24) and no incunable witness is recorded in the cited census and search surfaces. This paper presents a substrate-complete census of those nine witnesses: five stand-alone copies (Berlin SBB Ms. germ. qrt. 2021; Wolfenbüttel HAB Cod. 79 Aug. 2°; Wien ÖNB Cod. 2826; Nürnberg GNM Hs. 18792; Schloss Anholt, Salm-Salm Ms. 46), three witnesses that embed Hartlieb's plant chapters inside Konrad von Megenberg's Buch der Natur (Heidelberg UB Cpg 311; Michelstadt Nicolaus-Matz-Bibliothek Cod. D 684; Erbach Gräfliches Gesamthausarchiv Nr. 2), and one fragmentary stand-alone witness (Linz OÖ Landes-Kultur Ms. 4). Each witness is presented on a common codicological axis. The census is cross-referenced with the wider Hartlieb authorial corpus, which the Handschriftencensus author-record autoren/421 enumerates as 103 werk-entries across approximately 93–99 unique codices once Sammelband-internal overlap is deduplicated. The paper then frames the Kräuterbuch corpus as a structural comparator for the herbal section of Beinecke MS 408 (the Voynich Manuscript) at the level of production ecology only, with no identity inference, and explicitly distinguishes this framing from the authorship hypothesis of Brewer and Lewis (2024), which the project record disfavors on content-side grounds set out in §6.

title: The Wittelsbach–Burgundian Transalpine Physician Chain, 1413–1496 (with southern Frederician and northern print-tradition extensions)
abstract: This paper traces a transalpine court-physician chain whose Confirmed-tier coverage runs from the start of the Cermisone Padua professorship (1413) through the latest dated Generation-2 vernacular witness (1496), with Candidate-tier extensions to the Constitutions of Melfi (1231) at the southern end and the Upper-Rhine surgical print-tradition reception (1583) at the northern end. The keystone is Johannes Hartlieb's Padua doctorate of 11 May 1439 [1], anchored at scholarly-consensus level by Fürbeth's 1992 Untersuchungen zu Leben und Werk monograph (Hermaea NF 64, Niemeyer Tübingen, pp. 30–41), which links a Bavaria-Munich Wittelsbach court physician directly to the teaching faculty of Antonio Cermisone and Bartolomeo Montagnana. Around that keystone we read a nine-manuscript witness cluster (1429–1496) carrying iatromathematisches Hausbuch, Regimen sanitatis, and Speculum humanae salvationis calendrical material across a German-vernacular regional book culture spanning Bavaria, Bodensee, Konstanz, Heidelberg, and Bohemian-Silesian production sites [2]. At publisher/imprint level, the separately compiled Bolt corpus describes approximately 1,000 apothecaries in roughly 85 Burgundian-state towns between 1200 and 1600 [3]; the exact internal count of 1,029 remains unreproduced here. The Avicenna Canon (Gerard of Cremona Latin) supplies a 14th–15th-century textual spine, carried in this study by seven Despars-stratum manuscripts in our holdings [4]. The Burgundian–Wittelsbach extension section engages the Brewer–Lewis 2024 Social History of Medicine paper as a methodologically valued, peer-reviewed precedent that correctly identifies Hartlieb's Bavaria-Munich service but does not extend the Wittelsbach reading across the Bavaria-Straubing maternal-line dynastic bridge into the Burgundian court. The paper closes with a programmatic register of the corridor's unexploited cross-connections to the Doutrepont–De Winter–Wijsman–Falmagne–Vaughan Burgundian-library bibliography and to the Bolt apothecary corpus. The thesis is comparator-lens, not identity. We do not claim that the chain produced Beinecke MS 408; we claim that the chain is a substrate-anchored object whose members, dates, teacher–student edges, and manuscript witnesses are attested at primary-source or scholarly-consensus level (the keystone doctorate date at the latter; see the keystone date section) and bracket the relevant fifteenth-century medical-book economy with sufficient density to be read as a stratum in its own right.

title: Descriptive Opener-Class Structure in the Voynich Manuscript Balneological Section (f75r–f84v)
abstract: This successor retains the twenty-folio count table and four-zone description and adds the missing tie-sensitivity replay. Two folios are tied: f78r at q=11 and s=11, and f79r at q=10 and s=10. Across all four admissible tie resolutions, G ranges from 11 to 13 and the one-sided Monte Carlo permutation value ranges from 0.00048 to 0.02284 at 100,000 trials per configuration. The uniform-label null is therefore rejected at 0.05 under every tie resolution. This does not distinguish the proposed regimen from a another topically structured arrangement. The s-to-q-to-o-to-s treatment sequence remains Candidate and lacks an independent period-source witness. The balneological section of the Voynich Manuscript (f75r–f84v, 20 folios) has been read as bathing imagery, gynecological imagery, or an alchemical process. This paper reports a class-opener extraction over the identified IVTFF file and evaluates a four-zone rule defined in the Methods. Under the alphabetical tie rule, the script records G=13/20 against a 10,000-shuffle null (mean 6.13, SD 1.93, corrected one-sided empirical p=0.0007). The observed dominant-class sequence is: Zone 1, three s-dominant and one o-dominant folio; Zone 2, six q-dominant folios; Zone 3, three o-, two q-, and one p-dominant folio; Zone 4, one s-dominant folio followed by three q-dominant folios. These are script outputs under the internal class labels, not plaintext meanings. The f79v midpoint description and its figure labels come from the internal image audit and remain descriptive. A former working-note claim that Conciliator labels occur on all 20 folios is not retained. This packet contains no exported query receipt, detection threshold, or off-section base rate for that claim; P-004 and the Paduan dataset are program-context and priority references only. The partial image taxonomy assigns 12 of 20 folios to COMMUNAL POOL, CASE ENTRY, or CATALOG ROW categories and leaves eight unbucketed. The s→q→o→s phase interpretation is an internal workflow hypothesis situated in P-009's corridor context, pending an off-section baseline and an independent medieval-source locus for the proposed order.

title: Recurrence plots in linguistics
abstract: Abstract This paper illustrates the use of recurrence plots as tools for linguistic analysis. We emphasize their potential to kickstart research into un(der)studied languages or linguistic data, focussing on ways of using them that require little linguistic preprocessing, needing only an audio recording of speech or a transcription with or without gloss (the first level of linguistic annotation that field linguists create). Recurrence plots can offer insight into the repetition, and repetition-with-variation, structures of these (relatively) raw linguistic materials, thus offering first inroads into the internal composition of even little- or un-annotated data. As an example, we work with audio and transcriptions from Igu, a language used solely for ritual purposes in the Kera’a-speaking community of Arunachal Pradesh (India). We show that recurrence plots are useful in highlighting specific aspects of repetition in the materials analysed.
venue: The European Physical Journal Special Topics

title: Socio-Cultural Transformation among the Dhangar Community in Solapur District
abstract: including Solapur district. The Dhangar Community has always had a connection with pastoralism, sheep and goat rearing moving with the seasons traditional jobs, family relationships, cultural activities and groups that work together.. Over time the way of life of the Dhangar Community has changed because of new money situations, more learning, cities growing new tools being used the environment changing and new jobs becoming available. These changes have led to changes in the way the Dhangar Community lives and how they are organized socially and culturally. This study wants to look at the changes happening in the cultural way of life of the Dhangar Community in Solapur district. It pays attention to changes in family setups how people get married, family connections, what jobs people do what they hope to learn what roles men and women play, religious activities, celebrations, traditions what they eat what they wear and how they get along with others in the community. The study also wants to find out how the members of the Dhangar Community deal with traditions and new ways of living. The research will use a method that involves going into the field and getting first-hand information from interviews watching what people do filling out questionnaires and talking with some people from the Dhangar Community. Information from sources will help understand the past how many people there are, the social side and the culture of the Dhangar Community. The study will pay attention to differences between older people and younger people and to what happens in homes where people have changed jobs or moved away. This study expects to show that the changes happening in the Dhangar Community are not about giving up old ways or just taking on new ways. Instead these changes are about adapting and finding a way to mix traditions the way the community sees itself and new goals that people have for their lives. The study could help people understand more about how the lives of people who live by herding animalsre changing. It could also offer ideas for programs and plans, about learning, jobs helping people live better and keeping traditions alive in Solapur district.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Interior Design: Opportunities, Challenges and Future Perspectives
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming the design industry by introducing data-driven, generative, predictive, and automated approaches to creative and technical processes. Interior design, traditionally dependent on human creativity, spatial understanding, material knowledge, and client preferences, is increasingly influenced by AI-powered tools capable of generating design concepts, visualizations, layouts, material combinations, lighting solutions, and personalized spatial recommendations. Recent developments in generative AI, machine learning, computer vision, natural language processing, and multimodal systems have expanded the possibilities for designers to explore a larger number of alternatives in less time. This research paper examines the opportunities, challenges, and future perspectives associated with the integration of Artificial Intelligence into interior design. The study adopts a qualitative systematic literature review approach and synthesizes recent research on AI-assisted architectural and built-environment design. The review indicates that AI can support concept generation, space planning, 3D visualization, material selection, sustainability analysis, personalization, and client communication. However, issues related to creativity, algorithmic bias, intellectual property, data privacy, professional responsibility, design authenticity, technical skills, and overdependence on automated systems remain significant challenges. Recent systematic reviews show that AI research in design is strongly concentrated in early conceptual and schematic stages, while later stages requiring detailed technical, contextual, and professional judgment remain comparatively underexplored. The paper argues that AI should not be viewed as a replacement for interior designers but as an augmentation technology that can strengthen human creativity, decision-making, and productivity. A human-centred AI framework combining technological capability with professional expertise, ethical safeguards, cultural sensitivity, and user participation is proposed. The study concludes that the future of interior design will increasingly depend on effective human–AI collaboration rather than complete automation.

title: Rethinking The Paithani Handloom Economy In Maharashtra
abstract: Abstract Paithani is simultaneously a heritage textile, a livelihood system and a differentiated market product. This paper develops a new analytical framework for understanding the contemporary Paithani handloom economy in Maharashtra by connecting four dimensions that are often examined separately: cluster structure, production economics, market access and authenticity. The analysis is based on the supplied study of the Yeola and Paithan clusters and reorganizes its evidence into a business-oriented interpretation rather than reproducing its original structure. The source describes more than 12,000 active handloom weavers and auxiliary workers, annual production above 85,000 authentic handloom sarees, and a strong concentration of commercial activity in Yeola. It also identifies substantial differences between the cost of authentic handwoven products and powerloom imitations. The paper argues that the central economic problem is not simply competition from cheaper substitutes; it is the difficulty of converting craftsmanship, time and authenticity into a price that is transparent and understandable to consumers. GI protection, digital direct-to-consumer channels, traceability, raw-material support and design innovation therefore need to operate as a connected strategy. The paper concludes with a practical framework for strengthening artisan bargaining power while protecting the identity of Paithani.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Sustainable Futures and Literary Voices: Eco-Criticism in the Age of AI
abstract: Abstract: The accelerating climate crisis and the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) have created a new intellectual landscape in which environmental sustainability no longer be discussed independently of technological development. Literature, as a cultural form capable of representing ecological relationships, technological anxieties, and alternative futures, has an important role in this debate. This paper examines how contemporary ecocriticism respond to the environmental challenges associated with artificial intelligence while also exploring the potential of AI to support environmental knowledge, literary interpretation, and sustainable futures. Drawing upon ecocritical theory, environmental humanities, posthumanism, Indigenous ecological thought, and recent scholarship on AI and environmental sustainability, the study analyses selected works including Margaret Atwood’s Oryx and Crake, Amitav Ghosh’s The Great Derangement, Richard Powers’s The Overstory, Robin Wall Kimmerer’s Braiding Sweetgrass, and Donna J. Haraway’s Staying with the Trouble. The paper argues that these texts challenge anthropocentric assumptions by foregrounding interdependence among humans, nonhuman organisms, technologies, and ecological systems. Atwood exposes the destructive consequences of technological mastery; Ghosh identifies the limitations of literary forms that marginalize ecological catastrophe; Powers expands narrative attention from individual human lives to forests and multispecies networks; Kimmerer proposes reciprocity rather than domination as the basis of ecological ethics; and Haraway advocates “making-with” other species rather than seeking technological mastery over nature.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Building an Egalitarian Society and Sustainable Development: A Study of Dr. Ambedkar's Thoughts
abstract: Abstract: The concept of sustainable development is very important in modern times. In sustainable development, importance is given to socio-economic and environmental development. 17 goals have been identified to achieve sustainable development. While considering these goals, the sustainability of Dr. Ambedkar's thoughts is also being highlighted. His thoughts also reflect various aspects of sustainability such as poverty eradication, inequality eradication, good health and welfare, quality education, gender equality, and economic growth. The main objective of this research paper is to study how useful Dr. Ambedkar's thoughts are in this concept. Descriptive and analytical research methods have been adopted for the presented research paper. Also, secondary sources have been used as a source of information. When considered in the context of sustainable development, Dr. Ambedkar's thoughts are analogous to the goals of sustainable development. If sustainable development is to be achieved, it is possible to create an equitable, just, and inclusive society by keeping Dr. Ambedkar's thoughts in mind; therefore, Dr. Ambedkar's thoughts are as effective and useful today as they were then. Dr. Ambedkar's thoughts are still a guide for creating an egalitarian society. In the present research paper, when the goal of sustainable development and the thoughts of Dr. Ambedkar are studied, it is found that out of the 17 goals of sustainable development, Dr. Ambedkar's thoughts show similarity with 10 goals. Therefore, even in contemporary times, Dr. Ambedkar's thoughts are still guiding and useful for the welfare of society, for eliminating inequality in society, establishing economic equality, and preserving human dignity.

title: Plight of the Oppressed and Ambedkrian Efforts: A critical study of Considering Babytai's autobiography.
abstract: Abstract: The downtrodden and their suffering are the main issues handled by authors. Dalit literature is the evidence of Dalit community arduous efforts for existence. The intention of Dalit authors to reveal the plight of the oppressed community and Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar countless efforts to bring them out mainstream. Nowadays number of Dalit writer's centering the ideas of Ambedkar's philosophy and ideology. The main objective of Dalit writing is Dalit people should be treated with respect and dignity. Babytai's writing is a testimony of the pivotal position of Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar in shaping Indian Dalit thoughts and customs. He had played a vital role to transform Dalits which is kindly observed in their writing. Thus, through this research paper, an attempt has been made to bring forth the arduous efforts of Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar to change the condition of Dalit community especially women.

title: Women, Climate Crisis, And Sustainable Futures: An Ecofeminist Reading of Barbara Kingsolver's Flight Behavior and Octavia E. Butler's Parable Of The Sower
abstract: Abstract Contemporary American literature increasingly responds to the ecological crises generated by climate change, environmental degradation, resource depletion, social inequality, and unsustainable human practices. Barbara Kingsolver’s Flight Behavior (2012) and Octavia E. Butler’s Parable of the Sower (1993) offer powerful literary representations of societies confronting environmental instability and its social consequences. Although the novels differ significantly in genre, historical context, and narrative form, both place women at the centre of ecological and social transformation. This paper examines the representation of women, nature, climate crisis, environmental justice, and sustainable futures in the two novels through an ecofeminist framework. It focuses particularly on Dellarobia Turnbow in Flight Behavior and Lauren Olamina in Parable of the Sower, arguing that their experiences reveal the interconnectedness of environmental exploitation, patriarchal structures, economic inequality, and social vulnerability. In Kingsolver’s novel, the unexpected arrival of monarch butterflies in rural Appalachia becomes a visible manifestation of climate disruption and a catalyst for Dellarobia’s intellectual and personal awakening. In Butler’s dystopian narrative, climate change, drought, water scarcity, violence, economic collapse, and displacement create a world in which Lauren must develop new forms of survival and community. The paper further argues that both novels move beyond representations of ecological catastrophe by imagining possibilities for resilience, ecological consciousness, collective responsibility, and sustainable futures. Their concerns correspond particularly with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, including gender equality, reduced inequalities, sustainable communities, responsible consumption, and climate action. Through a comparative ecofeminist reading, this study demonstrates that contemporary American literature can function as an important cultural space for interrogating environmental injustice and imagining alternative relationships between women, society, and the natural world.

title: Visions of Tomorrow: Literary Cartographies of Vikasit Bharat@2047 in Indian and Anglophone Literatures
abstract: Abstract The national discourse surrounding Vikasit Bharat@2047 envisions India’s centenary of independence through economic self-reliance, technological transcendence, sustainability, and socio-cultural rejuvenation. While socioeconomic frameworks dominate state policy, the literature serves as an essential barometer of civilizational ethos and human experience. This study investigates how Indian literature—both in English and translated regional vernaculars—imagines, interrogates, and constructs pathways toward a developed India by 2047. Drawing on postcolonial theory, speculative realism, ecocriticism, and subaltern studies, this study analyzes how contemporary and visionary literary works negotiate the tensions between hyper-modernity and ancient philosophical inheritances (Sanatana ethics, Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam). It interrogates the themes of technological ethics, ecological stewardship, gender democratization and subaltern emancipation. Ultimately, this paper argues that Indian literature does not merely reflect developmental milestones; it actively provides an ethical and philosophical blueprint for Vikasit Bharat, ensuring that material progress remains tethered to human dignity and ecological equilibrium.

title: The Gandhikas: Perfumers in Early India
abstract: Abstract In early India fragrances played a significant role in everyday life and were used in many social, religious and personal contexts. However, the people who made and sold these fragrances are often less discussed. This paper highlights the Gandhikas who were Perfumers and Perfume sellers who were mentioned in early Indian literary and inscriptional sources. It examines the nature of their work and other aromatic substances associated with their occupation. Buddhist and Jain texts along with inscriptions from Mathura and Western Deccan provide glimpses into the presence and activities of Gandhikas and their position in the society. They also actively participated in religious donations which gives an insight into their economic circumstances and their connections with the urban communities. Hence the paper not only presents Gandhikas as mere perfume sellers but skilled artisans with knowledge of fragrant substances whose work was connected to religion, trade and everyday use of fragrance in early India.

title: Climate Crisis in Amitav Ghosh's Writings: With Special Reference to 'The Great Derangement' and 'Gun Island'
abstract: Abstract Climate change is one of the biggest problems facing the world in the twenty-first century. Rising temperatures, irregular rainfall, rising sea levels, floods, storms, droughts, and other natural disasters are changing both nature and human life. Science explains these changes through facts, data, and reports, but literature helps people understand their emotional and human effects. Literature can show fear, loss, displacement, and responsibility in ways that numbers alone cannot. This research paper studies two important works by Amitav Ghosh: The Great Derangement: Climate Change and the Unthinkable (2016) and the novel Gun Island (2019). In The Great Derangement, Ghosh asks why modern literature and politics have not responded strongly enough to climate change. He says that this failure is not only scientific or political but also a failure of culture and imagination. In Gun Island, he uses a story that combines myth, history, animal movement, environmental change, migration, and human suffering. The study shows that Ghosh does not see climate change as only a scientific problem. He connects it with colonial history, fossil-fuel use, capitalism, inequality, and human greed. He also presents nature as an active force that can affect and change human life. The paper concludes that Ghosh’s writings help readers understand the Anthropocene and encourage people to respect nature, understand climate justice, and accept collective responsibility for protecting the environment.

title: Feminist Perspectives in Preeti Shenoy's The One You Cannot Have: Agency, Patriarchy, and Female Identity
abstract: Abstract This research paper examines feminist perspectives in Preeti Shenoy's novel The One You Cannot Have (2013), analysing how the text negotiates women's agency, patriarchal constraints, and female identity within contemporary Indian society. Through close reading of the three female protagonists Shruti, Anjali, and Dipika this study explores how Shenoy presents women navigating tradition and modernity, love and duty, personal desire and social expectation. Drawing on feminist literary theory, the paper argues that while the novel operates within popular romance fiction, it offers a nuanced critique of patriarchal structures, particularly through its exploration of marriage, reproductive autonomy, female friendship, and work-life dilemmas.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: A Speech Act Analysis of Sudeep Nagarkar's It Started With a Friend Request
abstract: Abstract This paper analyses Sudeep Nagarkar’s popular romance novel It Started With a Friend Request (2013) through Speech Act Theory by J.L Austin and John Searle. The book is set in the contemporary urban relationship mediated by digital communication platforms and provides a rich corpus for studying how language works not only as description but as action. This paper conducts a close reading of the novel’s dialog, text messages, BBM chats and narrative voice and demonstrates how different speech acts declarations of love, promises, accusations, apologies, threats and rejections are performed by the characters to constitute and transform their relationships. The analysis reveals how digital communication platforms create new contexts for performative utterances, how the narrative structure employs performative language to construct intimacy and conflict, and how speech acts serve as the primary mechanism for relationship formation, maintenance, and dissolution in the novel. The paper argues that Nagarkar's novel, despite its popular fiction status, offers significant insights into the performative nature of contemporary romantic discourse in digitally mediated spaces.

title: "Women's Struggle And Strength In Select Novels Of Jai Nimbkar And Bharati Mukherjee "
abstract: Abstract Jai Nimbkar and Bharati Mukherjee both are Indian female writers. But Bharati Mukherjee is American writer of Indian origin. Jai Nimbkar was born in Pune and daughter of Dinesh Karwe and Irawati Karwe. She is feminist writer and wrote three novels in her life .Temporary Answer, A Joint Venture and Come Rain these are three novels which indicates women’s struggle, man-woman relationship. Her novel shows Women's position in patriarchal society. Bharati Mukherjee is Indian diasporic writer in the united states who was born in Calcutta but after some years she migrated to U. S. She has written eight novels and two collections of short stories such as ‘Darkness ’and ‘The Middleman and Other Stories’. Her earliest novels the Tiger's Daughter , Wife, Jasmine, Leave it to me, Desirable Daughters , Holder of The World , Miss New India and The Tree Bride these novels indicates cross cultural experiences , women's struggle and strength their own experiences through these novels from her experience as immigrant in the United States.

title: Fictionalizing History and Anthropology: A Case study of The Calcutta Chromosome
abstract: Abstract The present paper examines the relationship between fictionalizing history, novel and anthropology. The Calcutta Chromosome deals with medical history, Ronald Ross’s discovery of the malaria puzzle, computer applications, indigenous society, religious cults, tribal society, superstitions, counter science, silence as religion and the belief in the self-contradictory knowledge set against the background of nineteenth and twentieth century India.

title: False Prophecy and Prophetic Ethics: A Contextual Exegetical Analysis of Jeremiah 23:26-32 and Its Relevance to The Christ Apostolic Church, Nigeria
abstract: Prophecy holds a vital role in biblical tradition, serving as a channel for conveying God’s will, guidance, warnings, and instructions to His people. However, alongside genuine prophetic ministry, the Scriptures also highlight the existence of false claims where human ideas masquerade as divine revelations. In Jeremiah 23:26-32, this tension is addressed by calling out prophets whose messages originate from their hearts, rely on misleading dreams, misappropriate divine words, and assert divine authority without true commissioning. This study addresses these challenges and their significance for prophetic ministry within the Christ Apostolic Church (CAC). By employing a historical-grammatical and contextual exegetical approach, the study examined the historical and literary context, key Hebrew terms, rhetorical flow, and the theological and ethical implications of Jeremiah 23:26-32. The findings identified five key criteria for authentic prophecy: a divine source, fidelity to revelation, truthfulness, genuine commissioning, and communal benefit. The study concluded that false prophecy extends beyond making inaccurate predictions; it involves the deceptive presentation of human ideas as divine messages, which can lead to spiritual and communal damage. It recommended enhancing biblical and theological training, fostering scriptural and ecclesial discernment, ensuring ministerial accountability, promoting financial transparency, establishing ethical guidelines for sensitive prophetic issues, and increasing congregational education. The CAC should maintain its prophetic legacy by rooting prophetic ministry in Scripture, integrity, accountability, and service to God’s people, rather than in personal authority, manipulation, or financial gain.
venue: International Journal of Multidisciplinary and Innovative Research

title: Gandhi in the age of Social Media: Digital Activism, Misinformation and the challenge of Peaceful Resistance in Online Spaces
abstract: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi's philosophy of non-violent resistance has influenced global movements for over a century. However, in today's digital era, his principles encounter unique challenges. This paper explores how Gandhi's core ideas of Satyagraha, ahimsa, and moral persuasion translate to social media activism while facing issues like algorithmic amplification, misinformation, polarisation, and digital violence. By analysing contemporary movements and case studies, it argues that while Gandhi's ideas remain relevant for digital activism, they must be adapted to tackle the specific challenges of online spaces. The conflict between Gandhi's focus on truth and the engagement-driven nature of algorithms creates a critical dilemma for modern activists. This paper examines both the opportunities and limitations of Gandhian nonviolence in a world where algorithms influence discourse, misinformation spreads rapidly, and peaceful movements are exposed to new kinds of digital violence.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Reflections of Crime in Peter Robinson's Novel : A Necessary End
abstract: Abstract Peter Robinson's "A Necessary End" (1989), the third book in his Inspector Banks series, marks a major step forward for the British police procedural genre. This study focuses on Robinson's use of crime fiction as a medium to examine the interrelations between political activism, police violence, trauma, and moral complexity in Thatcherite Britain. By analyzing the characters and the story line, and through a thematic approach, this paper demonstrates that Robinson elevates detective fiction above its standard tropes by portraying crime as symptomatic rather than anomalous of broader societal rifts. The portrayal of politics in northern England during the 1980s, including issues of nuclear disarmament, police power, and alternative subcultures, provides a clear example of how crime fiction can be used as serious social criticism.

title: The Portrayal of Women in the Short Stories of Bharati Mukherjee
abstract: Abstract Mukherjee is a feminist writer in a true sense because she not only advocates feminism in her literary creations but her personal life is an evidence of it because she practices what she preaches. She discovers her identity at an early age and realizes that patriarchy is deeply ingrained in Indian culture. Bharati Mukherjee has been accredited as a writer of immigrants; the predominant fact about her literary works is that her works are female centered and about immigrant women. The maiden novel of Mukherjee, The Tiger’s Daughter, is autobiographical in nature because the protagonist Tara is like her who returns to India after seven years stay in America. Tara’s Indian relatives condemn her marriage with a foreigner, named David and criticize her decision of coming alone to India without the company of her husband. Mukherjee presents the evolution of the female characters from muteness to voice. The affirmation in their behaviour arises due to the amalgamation of two cultures; first of their native land culture and second of the host society’s culture. As most of the female characters hail from the Indian sub-continent so Indian patriarchal culture affects their lives but when they come into the contact of the liberated Western culture then ‘a new woman’ arises who seeks for ‘individual identity’. The quest for identity results in the assertion of their identities. Some of the female protagonists assert their identities while other swing in-between the two worlds and in the end take shelter of their old native land culture.

title: WP_019 Will and Geometric Representation: Schopenhauer's Blind Impulse as a Vacuum Fluctuation Model in Calabi-Yau Manifolds / 意志與幾何表象:叔本華盲目衝動在卡拉比-丘流形中的真空漲落模型
abstract: WP_019: Will and Geometric Representation: Schopenhauer's Blind Impulse as a Vacuum Fluctuation Model in Calabi-Yau Manifolds 意志與幾何表象:叔本華盲目衝動在卡拉比-丘流形中的真空漲落模型 Abstract / 摘要This paper establishes a rigorous physical and philosophical isomorphism between Arthur Schopenhauer's metaphysics of the Will (Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung) and the compactified vacuum physics of superstring theory. We demonstrate that Schopenhauer's "Thing-in-Itself Will"—the blind, aimless, and relentless drive behind all existence—finds its exact quantum gravitational manifestation in the unoriented, non-local zero-point vacuum fluctuations (rho_vac) within six-dimensional compactified Calabi-Yau manifolds (K6). The empirical world of "Representation" (Vorstellung) is formulated as low-energy effective field projections (L_4D^eff) resulting from string compactifications and non-perturbative flux potentials V(T, U). By deconstructing physical matter into temporary, metastable topological moduli fluctuations, this model provides a geometric foundation for eradicating the Three Poisons (Greed, Hatred, Delusion). It equips contemplative practitioners with a theoretical framework for cultivating radical renunciation (Nirveda) and transmuting blind, karma-driven impulses into the open-loop wisdom and compassion of Tathāgatagarbha. 本篇論文建立了亞瑟·叔本華(Arthur Schopenhauer)意志形上學(《作為意志與表象的世界》)與超弦理論緊緻化真空物理學之間嚴密的物理與哲學同構。我們論證了叔本華的「物自身意志」——驅動一切存在的盲目、無目的且永不停息的衝動——在六維緊緻化卡拉比-丘流形(K6)內部未定向、非定域的零點真空漲落(rho_vac)中找到了精確的量子引力體現。 經驗世界的「表象」(Vorstellung)則被形式化為由超弦緊緻化與非微擾通量勢能 V(T, U) 所導出的低能有效場投影(L_4D^eff)。透過將物理物質拆解為暫時性、亞穩態的拓撲模態漲落,本模型為斷除「貪、嗔、癡」三毒提供了幾何學根基,並為觀修實證者提供了一套理論框架,用以修習徹骨的「厭離心」(Nirveda),並將盲目、業力驅動的衝動轉化為如來藏的開環悲智願力。

title: Issues of Cultural Displacement and Intergenerational Conflict in Jhumpa Lahiri's'The Namesake'
abstract: Abstract The Namesake by Jhumpa Lahiri is a story about identity, family and the cultural assimilation. The book describes the life of Gogol Ganguli, the child of Indian immigrants, as he faces the obstacles of growing up in America while remaining connected to his Bengali (native) roots. The novel explores themes of belonging, separation and the significance of names in shaping one’s identity.The author deeply investigates the immigrant experience, generational tensions and the interaction between tradition and modernity through Gogol's conflicts regarding his name and cultural duality. The story expresses the intricate complexities of self-discovery amid conflicting cultural expectations.

title: History, Heritage, and Cultural Consciousness in Sudha Murthy's "Gently Falls the Bakula."
abstract: Abstract: The novel “Gently Falls the Bakula” by Sudha Murthy intricately explores various themes like relationships, marriage, gender, and human values, but one important aspect is the protagonist's historical view, which is represented by Sudha Murthy herself. Shrimati, an intellectual girl from a small town, loves history, believes in history, worships history, follows history, and admires history; sometimes it seems that she can’t live without it. The story centres on Shrimati, who, out of love for Shrikant, attempts to live without history; however, this sacrifice appears to render her love for Shrikant futile, leading to a loss of her identity. According to her, history taught her to follow the promises and sacrifice her life for Shrikant; his happiness is more than her choice or interest. She believes a sacrifice creates history; she respects Indian cultural heritage, and it is one of the most ancient and glorious histories and cultures in the world. By preserving and respecting our culture, it's a wonderful tribute to our history.

title: Resuscitating Culture through Translation: A Metalinguistic Reading of Valli in Malayalam and English
abstract: Resuscitating Culture through Translation: A Metalinguistic Reading of Valli in Malayalam and English First Author: Sangeetha G. NairSecond Authror: Dr. Sageera M.P Translation is often perceived as a mode of adaptation or transcreation from a source text to another, pertaining to its essence and facilitating cultural acclimation and hybridity. It is not a simple paraphrasing or rewording of the original text into a target language, but rather a creative reconstruction and a re-interpretation, embracing the dynamic nature of language as well as the human experience. It is a process where the translator enjoys the privilege of assimilating or rejecting whatever content he/she finds culturally, socially, linguistically and politically inappropriate. Translation thus becomes a creative adaptation and cultural re-contextualization, where the translator becomes a linguistic mediator as well as a creator of a metalanguage during the process. Literary translation plays a significant role in cross-cultural understanding and the transmission of cultural narratives, myths, and histories, keeping in mind a global audience. In the multilingual, multicultural landscape of India, translation has an evolutionary potential to integrate local ecologies and cultural contexts that can promote multiethnic exchanges and metalinguistic awareness. This paper intends to explore how translation becomes a transformative process of meaning-making, negotiation and cultural innovation in contemporary Malayalam fiction translated into English. This study attempts to throw light on the translation strategies adopted by Jayasree Kalathil in her English translation of the Malayalam novel Valli authored by Sheela Tomy, in encapsulating the tribal culture as well as the language, enabling visibility, adaptability and inclusiveness from a global perspective.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Reimagining English Studies: Interdisciplinary Research, Innovation, Culture, Governance and Sustainable Development in the Digital Age
abstract: Abstract English Studies has undergone a significant transformation in response to technological change, cultural mobility, environmental concerns and new forms of social and political communication. No longer confined to the study of canonical literary texts and language systems, the discipline increasingly intersects with cultural studies, environmental humanities, digital humanities, political discourse, education, media studies and questions of social responsibility. This paper examines how English Studies can contribute to the contemporary interdisciplinary agenda of research, innovation, culture, governance and sustainable development. The paper proposes an interdisciplinary L-L-C-G-S framework—Language, Literature, Culture, Governance and Sustainability—as a conceptual model for reimagining the role of English departments in higher education. Through qualitative analysis of selected literary and non-literary texts, including the poetry of William Wordsworth, Shakespearean drama, George Orwell’s writings and Amitav Ghosh’s climate-oriented fiction and nonfiction, the study explores how literary language can illuminate ecological responsibility, political power, ethical leadership, cultural identity and social change. It also considers the possibilities offered by digital humanities, multilingual education, communication skills and emerging technologies. The paper argues that English Studies can function as a bridge between the humanities and other disciplines by developing critical literacy, cultural awareness, ethical reasoning, communication competence and responsible engagement with contemporary challenges. Such an approach can strengthen the contribution of the humanities to the Sustainable Development Goals while preserving the interpretative and humanistic foundations of literary study.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Language, Spirituality and Cultural Identity in Contemporary India: An Interdisciplinary Study of Arundhathi Subramaniam's When God Is a Traveller
abstract: Abstract: In modern Indian English poetry, the medium can be seen to be increasingly being used to negotiate issues of culture, identity, spirituality and belonging. When God Is a Traveller (2014) by Arundhathi Subramaniam is, therefore, an important and significant poem in this poetic topography as it is a poem of the sacred and the mundane, the Indian philosophical tradition and the present, the myth and the modern, the individual's uncertainty and spiritual quest. In this paper, the relationship between language, Subramaniam's spirituality and cultural identity is discussed in an interdisciplinary approach to language. It upholds the notion that language is not simply a means of articulating spiritual concepts but is a place where the contemporary Indian identity is negotiated and re-constructed. The language of Subramaniam, like his poetry, is distinctive, using a range of devices including diction, metaphor, imagery, cultural references, mythological allusions, irony, and the use of ordinary and sacred vocabulary to create a poetic idiom that defies the boundaries of the spiritual and the secular. Poems like ‘How Some Hindus Find Their Personal Gods', ‘Eight Poems for Shakuntala', ‘Benaras', ‘Bhakti' and ‘When God Is a Traveller' illustrate this reinterpretation of inherited cultural and spiritual traditions in a fresh, contemporary use of the English language. The study also examines how the journey is reoccurring as a metaphor for self-discovery, spiritual questioning and identity formation. The paper is a conclusion that Subramaniam's poetry is a dynamic expression of the present time's cultural awareness of Indians in which the space of English is flexible for negotiating tradition, modernity, spirituality and individual identity.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Cultural Hybridization in Modern Indian Writing English Literature
abstract: Abstract Cultural hybridization is a central feature of modern Indian English literature, reflecting the dynamic interaction between indigenous traditions and global influences. Emerging from the historical context of colonialism and evolving through postcolonial and globalized realities, Indian English literature demonstrates how cultural identities are continuously negotiated and redefined. This research article examines the role of cultural hybridization in shaping literary expression, thematic concerns, and narrative strategies in contemporary Indian English writing. It explores how authors creatively merge Indian cultural elements with Western literary forms to produce a distinctive and multifaceted literary tradition. The study focuses on key dimensions of hybridization, including linguistic innovation, diasporic identity, narrative experimentation, and the interplay between tradition and modernity. Writers such as Salman Rushdie, Arundhati Roy, Jhumpa Lahiri, Amitav Ghosh, and Kiran Desai illustrate how hybridization operates both as a thematic concern and as a stylistic device. Their works depict characters navigating multiple cultural spaces, often reflecting tensions between inherited traditions and modern global influences. Language itself becomes a site of hybridity, as English is infused with vernacular expressions, regional idioms, and cultural references, thereby challenging the dominance of Standard English. Drawing upon postcolonial theoretical frameworks, particularly the concept of hybridity as articulated by Homi K. Bhabha, the article argues that cultural hybridization is not merely a consequence of cultural contact but a productive and transformative process. It enables writers to resist cultural homogenization and assert unique identities within a global context. The findings reveal that hybridization enriches literary creativity, fosters cross-cultural understanding, and redefines the boundaries of Indian English literature. Ultimately, this study highlights the significance of cultural hybridization as a powerful force that shapes the evolving landscape of modern Indian English literature in an increasingly interconnected world.

title: Living Heritage to Contemporary Design: Reinterpreting Madhubani Motifs for Sustainable Textile and Home Décor Applications
abstract: Abstract Madhubani painting, also known as Mithila painting, represents a rich visual tradition in which motifs, colours, symbols and narrative forms have been transmitted across generations. Traditionally associated with the Mithila region of Bihar, the art form has moved beyond its original contexts and has acquired wider visibility through changing materials, markets, exhibitions and contemporary design applications. The study investigates how selected Madhubani motifs can be interpreted and translated into contemporary textile and home décor products while retaining their cultural visual identity. The research connects visual arts, textile design, product development and cultural sustainability. The study argues that such reinterpretation can contribute to cultural sustainability by keeping traditional visual knowledge visible and usable in present-day contexts. At the same time, the paper distinguishes cultural sustainability from environmental sustainability because the source project used cotton-based fabrics and commercially available Fevicryl acrylic colours and did not establish a complete environmental life-cycle assessment. The study therefore positions Madhubani-inspired product development as a pathway for cultural continuity, design innovation, product diversification and future sustainable design research.

title: Researching research: The impact of librarians in an artistic environment
abstract: This study examines the impact of a research library within a higher-education arts institution. It explores the effectiveness of library resources and uncovers the gaps that can often contribute to a lack of student success in an academic art environment. Library and Information literacy is often an overlooked resource within art education. This study, however, highlights how libraries work to encourage artistic success. Through interviews and observations, this study emphasizes engagement, student access points, and the need for faculty collaboration with librarians. The aim is to highlight the impact libraries can have on artistic student success, creating opportunities for a more diverse and accessible learning environment.
venue: The Journal of Academic Librarianship

title: The Banjara Legacy: How India's First Settlers, Traders, and Transporters, Pioneered Indus Valley Urbanism., First Migrants, First Pastoralists, and First Farmers
abstract: By linking Sir John Marshall’s foundational stratigraphic records with Darwinian adaptive principles, this study proves that the ancestral Banjara community—operating as the prehistoric Pani and Gorvamsha traders—built an unbroken 6,000-to-8,000-year logistical legacy that pioneered and sustained Indus Valley urbanism through cross-continental trade This paper posits that the Banjara community constitutes the foundational socio-economic bedrock of ancient Indian civilization, functioning as the primary catalysts for human advancement in the Indian subcontinent. Rather than viewing nomadic and sedentary cultures as historical opposites, this study argues that the ancestral Banjaras underwent a systematic, sequential evolution. They transitioned from the subcontinent’s first indigenous settlers and seasonal migrants into its pioneering pastoralists and early farmers. This evolutionary trajectory culminated in their role as the premier trans-regional traders and logistics providers whose organized networks directly underpinned and populated the first planned urban centers of the Indus Valley Civilization. Interdisciplinary evidence supporting this transformation spans ancestral migratory pathways, early zooarchaeological records of cattle domestication, and material culture distributions. Central to this thesis is the antiquity of the pack-bullock transport system—an overland supply-chain infrastructure uniquely perfected by the Banjaras' ancestral transport guilds (Tandas). Spatial mapping reveals that prehistoric campsites in resource-extraction zones directly align with traditional Banjara transit corridors. This indicates an undeniable structural overlap between proto-historic nomadic logistics and the economic surpluses found within planned Indus cities. Analyzing these connections reveals that nomadic logistics mastery served as the vital connective tissue making South Asian urban ecosystems possible. The ancestral Banjara network bridged the gap between mobile resource zones and fixed urban markets, sustaining a specialized, non-agricultural urban population. Thus, the "Indus Urbanite" was an evolution of the highly organized mobile trader. Ultimately, this study rebalances historical discourse by challenging sedentary-biased narratives. By demonstrating that mobile transport guilds were central to ancient state-building, this paper directly links the very roots of South Asian urbanization to the enduring legacy of the Banjaras.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: From Ritual Walls to Contemporary Spaces: Reimagining Warli Visual Heritage through Contemporary Artistic Mediums
abstract: Abstract Warli art, traditionally practiced by Warli communities of Maharashtra and adjoining regions, is one of India’s distinctive indigenous visual languages. Emerging from ritual practices, seasonal celebrations, agricultural cycles, and community narratives, it has historically functioned as more than aesthetic expression: it has carried collective memory, social communication, ecological awareness, and cultural identity. Its movement from ritual wall paintings in domestic and ceremonial spaces to galleries, urban interiors, digital platforms, public murals, and commercial products reflects an ongoing relationship between tradition and innovation. This paper examines the transformation of Warli visual heritage through contemporary artistic mediums. It considers the geometric vocabulary, narrative structures, ecological consciousness, and indigenous knowledge embedded in Warli imagery and examines their adaptation into contemporary painting, murals, installation, fashion, digital media, architecture, interior design, and product design. The paper argues that Warli art should not be understood merely as a decorative folk style, but as a living knowledge system whose meanings can engage with present-day cultural, social, and environmental concerns. At the same time, commercialization raises questions of authenticity, cultural ownership, attribution, and artistic agency. The paper therefore proposes cultural continuity as a balance between preservation, creative transformation, and community participation.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Local And Regional History Of Ahilyanagar (Ahmednagar), Maharashtra
abstract: Abstract The Present Research Paper Examines The Local And Regional History Of Ahilyanagar (Historically Ahmednagar), Maharashtra, From Ancient Times To The Contemporary Period. Ahilyanagar Occupies An Important Position In The Political, Military, Social, Economic And Cultural History Of The Deccan. Its Geographical Location Between Important Centres Of The Deccan Contributed To Its Strategic And Historical Significance. The History Of The Region Extends To The Ancient Period, While The Foundation Of The City In 1494 By Malik Ahmad Nizam Shah I Marked A Major Turning Point. The City Subsequently Became The Capital Of The Nizam Shahi Sultanate And Developed Into An Important Centre Of Administration, Military Activity And Culture. The Region Later Witnessed Mughal Expansion, Maratha Political Activity And British Colonial Rule. The Study Gives Particular Attention To The Nizam Shahi Period, The Role Of Chand Bibi, Mughal-Nizam Shahi Conflicts, The Maratha Period, British Administration And Local Resistance Movements. It Also Examines The Participation Of The Region In The Indian Freedom Movement, Especially The Importance Of Ahilyanagar Fort As A Place Of Detention For Nationalist Leaders During The Quit India Movement. The Research Further Examines The Social, Economic And Cultural History Of The District, Its Architectural Heritage, Important Historical Personalities And The Changing Historical Identity Of The Region. The Study Concludes That Ahilyanagar's History Represents A Significant Part Of The Wider History Of Maharashtra And The Deccan.

title: Thematic Concerns and Existential Dimensions in the Poetry of Jayanta Mahapatra
abstract: Abstract Jayanta Mahapatra occupies a significant position in Indian English poetry because of the distinctive manner in which he combines personal experience, regional consciousness, historical memory, social observation, and existential reflection. His poetry frequently explores the individual’s encounter with loneliness, alienation, suffering, mortality, faith, desire, memory, and the uncertainties of human existence. At the same time, his poetic world remains deeply rooted in Odisha, its landscape, cultural traditions, religious practices, history, and ordinary social life. This paper examines the major thematic concerns and existential dimensions of Mahapatra’s poetry, with particular attention to alienation, loneliness, identity, death, suffering, memory, sexuality, spirituality, and the individual’s search for meaning. Poems such as “Hunger,” “Dawn at Puri,” “Indian Summer,” “A Rain of Rites,” “Relationship,” “Exile,” and other representative poems demonstrate how the personal and the geographical become interconnected in his poetic imagination. His treatment of religious imagery is particularly complex, bringing together spiritual questioning and cultural observation. His poetry also gives considerable attention to marginalized lives and the position of women within social structures. The paper argues that Mahapatra’s existential consciousness is not detached from Indian reality; rather, it emerges through landscape, history, culture, relationships, and everyday human experience. His poetry therefore presents existential uncertainty as both a deeply personal condition and a reflection of wider social and cultural realities.

title: Ecological Armageddon: Helon Habila's Oil on Water as a Legendary Voice
abstract: Abstract: In the modern period, capitalistic upheavals on Earth and the ensuing climate shifts seem to be major worldwide concerns brought on by unbridled materialistic pursuits. Oil on Water by Helon Habila tells the story of the ongoing suffering of Nigeria's Dehumanized Indigenous people. Nigeria was the world's tenth largest oil exporter. The abundant oil reserves resulted in widespread exploitation. The novel Oil on Water by the Nigerian writer Helon Habila deals with environmental pollution in the oil-rich Nigerian Delta. Corporate greed and hegemonic oppression have been the driving force behind environmental degradation and human exploitation. The lust for oil and high profit provoked the capitalist to go and occupy the most sought-after African countries, to show their supremacy over land, and to disregard environmental ethics. Hence, it becomes apt to mention Robert D. Bullard who said the following words to characterize the need for EJ: "Risk burdens are localized yet the benefits are generalized across all segments of society". This paper aims to prove the above said point with reference to Oil on Water which is set in the environmentally devastated Nigerian Delta.

title: Fragrances for the afterlife: four terracotta incense burners from LCG-2 corridor-shaped tomb at Dibbā al-Bayah (Sultanate of Oman)
abstract: The present contribution is concerned with four examples of terracotta incense burners found in tomb LCG-2 in Dibbā al-Bayah (Sultanate of Oman). Large Collective Grave 2 (LCG-2) is a corridor-shaped structure and is dated from the Middle Iron Age (1000-800 BC) to the PIR (Pré-Islamique Récente) period (250 BC-400 AD). Two of the artefacts belong to the category of decorated cuboid terracotta incense burners, which are widespread in Arabia and the Near and Middle East and represent the basic form of these containers. In contrast, the other two are original examples due to their small size, the decoration of their external surfaces, and the preservation of the lid in one of them. The following study sets out to provide a contextual framework for understanding the significance of the artefacts in question. To this end, it traces the tradition of incense burners in southern Arabia, and particularly the diffusion of this specific container from Dhofar to the northern coasts of the Oman Peninsula.

title: Children's Literature
abstract: Abstract It is worth noting that children’s literature is one of the rapidly growing fields in the literature on one hand, but on the other hand, it is also the most argumentative area of study among critics and all interested persons. children’s literature, the body of written works and accompanying illustrations produced in order to entertain or instruct young people. The genre encompasses a wide range of works, including acknowledged classics of world literature, picture books and easy-to-read stories written exclusively for children, and fairy tales, lullabies, fables, folk songs, and other primarily orally transmitted materials.Originating in didactic and moral instruction, the field has expanded to prioritise imaginative play, multimodal meaning-making and critical inquiry. Contemporary research highlights the role of visual narrative, typographic design and digital media in shaping narrative comprehension, while also interrogating issues of representation, environmental ethics and social justice. By fostering linguistic, visual and digital literacies, children’s literature serves as a vital site for empathy building, identity formation and global citizenship, with applications ranging from classroom pedagogy and teacher training to inclusive publishing and museum education.

title: The Relevance of "Puruṣartha" in Contemporary Life
abstract: Abstract ‘Puruṣartha’ literally means an entity of Human Pursuit for attainment of fulfillment in life . It is a key concept in Vedic civilization and refers to the four proper goals of human life. The four Puruṣarthas are Dharma, Artha, Kaama and Moksha. The ideas of Puruṣartha have played a very fundamental role in the mythological history of Indian deliberation. Every individual is expected to achieve these four Purushartha with detachment, without any expectation in human life. The purpose of Puruṣartha is to ensure that people would not neglect their obligatory means duties in their deluded state by becoming obsessed with particular desires that may lead to moral and social decadence and destruction of family values. To understand our goals of life we should not look outside, as to where the world is going, but should rather look within inner self, as to what do we really hope and want. In the modern world, society itself progress through the use of huge technological methods, forgetting the final destination of our life. Today modern human lifestyle has weakened the ultimate value of puruṣartha. This paper attempts to show the significance of the ideals of puruṣartha in human life as a guiding principle in all stages of life and also would explore the importance of puruṣartha knowledge that is still relevant to our modern life.
