title: Risk and uncertainty in digital preservation: A survey of CoreTrustSeal certified repositories
abstract: Digital repositories certified as trustworthy through systems such as CoreTrustSeal (CTS) are expected to demonstrate readiness for the ongoing work of long-term digital preservation. Yet certification processes rest on largely positivistic assumptions about risk: that risks can be identified, classified, and quantified, and that all parties will interpret risk information consistently. This article challenges that assumption by applying a social constructionist lens to examine how staff members from CTS certified repositories understand risk and characterize uncertainty in the context of digital preservation. Drawing on survey data from 88 respondents across the CTS community (a 54% response rate), the study uses qualitative coding to analyze open-ended responses about the most significant risks and uncertainties facing certified repositories. Findings show that respondents understood risk in terms of concrete threats across five categories: finance, legal, organizational infrastructure, repository processes, and technical infrastructure. Financial sustainability, staffing, and technical infrastructure were particularly prominent. Respondents characterized uncertainty in three areas: finance, data and infrastructure, and the Designated Community. Notably, sources of uncertainty were primarily external to the repository, and respondents frequently treated risk and uncertainty as overlapping or interchangeable concepts. These findings reveal that even repositories that have passed an external audit continue to face significant interconnected threats, particularly around the ability to sustain funding, retain expertise, and maintain infrastructure over time. The study contributes to information science scholarship by demonstrating that technical and procedural standards alone cannot address the complex challenges of digital preservation, and that attention to how practitioners construct meaning around risk is essential for improving both certification systems and preservation practice.
venue: Journal of Librarianship and Information Science

title: Residual Discovery as Open-World Scientific Search: From Anomaly Clusters to Testable Hypotheses Without Reusing Discovery Evidence
abstract: Model failure is the engine of scientific progress, but the transition from unexplained observation to testable hypothesis lacks a formal protocol. Posterior predictive checks (Box 1980; Gelman, Meng, and Stern 1996) identify model inadequacy; Bayesian nonparametric methods (Rasmussen 2000; Ferguson 1973) grow hypothesis spaces automatically; preregistration (Chambers 2013; Nosek et al. 2018) constrains post-hoc hypothesis revision and makes it detectable. None of the cited systems supplies the complete typed lifecycle defined here, from residual detection through bin formation, candidate registration, confirmatory evaluation, and versioned disposition. This paper develops a formal methodology for residual discovery as open-world scientific search. The framework begins with observations that are inadequately predicted by all active models. These observations enter an unresolved residual pool rather than being forced into the least-bad available explanation. Residuals may then be grouped into candidate bins according to recurrence, stability, coherence, and novelty. A candidate bin is not yet a hypothesis. It becomes one only when it is compressed into a predictive specification capable of making discriminating claims about unseen data.

title: The Role Of Socio-Cultural Criticism In Indian English Literature
abstract: Abstract The Indian English Literature has been constantly dealing with the intricate relationship between literature and society, culture, history and power, hence, Socio-cultural criticism takes a central position in the study of Indian English Literature. Literary texts by Indian English writers have not only captured social reality but also challenged caste systems, gender inequalities, colonialism, poverty, religious conflict, cultural conflict, modernity, globalization, migration and the evolving nature of Indian identity. In this article, the focus is on the socio-cultural criticism of selected writers of Indian English Literature such as Mulk Raj Anand, R. K. Narayan, Raja Rao, Anita Desai, Salman Rushdie, Arundhati Roy, Amitav Ghosh, Rohinton Mistry, Jhumpa Lahiri, and Kiran Desai. It suggests that in doing so, socio-cultural criticism can shed light on literature as a cultural document, as a place of ideological contestation, and as a site of visibility to the experiences of the margins. Caste, class, gender, nationalism, religion, language, tradition and modernity, diaspora, globalization and ecology have also been taken up into consideration in the discussion. To sum up, the study finds that socio-cultural criticism brings out a wider scope for literary interpretation by relating literary representation with the real life of Indian society and also by showcasing the role of Indian English Literature in the debate of the culture and the transformation of the society.

title: Human Imperfection and the Philosophy of Legal and Political Restraint
abstract: This paper posits that human beings are fundamentally imperfect entities driven by biological instincts and hedonistic pursuits. Challenging traditional theories that anchor the legitimacy of punishment in transcendental moral purity, this study redefines the law as a pragmatic social contract grounded in Mutually Assured Deterrence (MAD) and reciprocal risk. Drawing upon Plato's allegory of the 'Ring of Gyges' and modern political analysis, we examine the 'Power Revelation Phenomenon'—wherein absolute power does not merely corrupt, but unmasks inherent moral flaws once external restraints are removed. Finally, this framework is applied to contrast North Korean autocratic rule with democratic constitutional systems, clarifying the philosophical necessity of institutional checks and judicial reforms.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: CT-based hard-tissue craniofacial landmarks and paranasal sinuses for biological profile estimation (sex, age and stature) in human populations: a scoping review
abstract: Abstract Background Sex, age, and stature estimation are core tasks in forensic and biological anthropology. Computed tomography (CT)- and cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT)-based imaging now allows detailed measurement of craniofacial hard tissue and the paranasal sinuses for this purpose, but findings are scattered across different populations, imaging protocols, and analytic methods. Craniofacial landmarks are discrete, reproducible bony reference points on the skull used for standardised measurement, such as nasion, zygion, gonion, glabella, and porion. This scoping review mapped that evidence base using the Population, Concept, Context (PCC) framework: human subjects undergoing cranial or paranasal CT-based imaging (Population), CT-based craniofacial and sinus measurements (Concept), and forensic estimation of sex, age, or stature (Context). Main body Searches of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, from inception to 7 May 2026, identified 76 eligible studies from 18 countries, led by India (24), Brazil (11), and Iran (8). Screening was performed independently by two reviewers. The maxillary sinus was the most studied structure (55 studies), followed by the frontal (33) and sphenoid (14) sinuses; the ethmoid sinus appeared in only one study. Sex estimation dominated the literature (72 studies), age estimation was addressed in 16, and no study examined stature. Discriminant function analysis (DFA) remained the standard statistical approach, though machine learning (ML) methods performed comparably or better where tested. Sex-classification accuracy ranged from about 60% to over 96%, and external validation across populations was rare. Conclusion The evidence base for CT-based sex estimation is broad but fragmented by population-specific formulae and limited external validation. Evidence for age estimation is weaker, and stature estimation from these structures remains unstudied. Future work should prioritise standardised measurement protocols, cross-population validation, and research into stature estimation.
venue: Egyptian Journal of Forensic Sciences

title: A Multi‐Scale Collaborative Framework for Transforming Cultural Power in Traditional Villages Through Ecological Resilience: Evidence From Zhejiang Province, China
abstract: ABSTRACT Traditional villages are heritage settlements whose continuity depends on interactions among cultural practice, ecological condition and governance capacity. This study examined how cultural power and governance networks are associated with ecological resilience in nine traditional villages in Zhejiang Province, China. A mixed‐methods design combined remote‐sensing analysis, spatial overlay, social network modelling, cultural inventories, interviews and institutional document review. The dataset covered villages of 2.20–3.25 km 2 , elevations of 315–665 m, populations of 390–610 residents, Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) time series from 2015 to 2024, land‐use maps, 120 heritage structures, 52 ritual sites and interviews with 115 governance and community actors. Cultural Power Index (CPI) was calculated from cultural density, ritual continuity and custodian presence, whereas ecological resilience was assessed using NDVI, Ecological Index (EI), vegetation stability, flood exposure and spatial conflict zones. Type I villages showed stronger resilience profiles, whereas Type III villages showed weaker ecological performance and more fragmented governance. Regression and spatial lag modelling indicated that cultural density, ritual continuity, governance centrality and vertical coordination were positively associated with resilience, whereas tourism pressure and conflict‐zone overlap were negatively associated with resilience.

title: Automating the Morning Outfit Decision: A Cognitive-Load Framework for Product Experience Design in Everyday Dress
abstract: Choosing what to wear is one of the first and most frequently repeated decisions of the day, yet product design treats it either as a matter of taste or as a pretext for selling new garments. This paper argues that the morning outfit decision is a well-specified product experience problem: a bundle of interdependent micro-decisions performed under time pressure, over a large and poorly indexed choice set, with consequences for how the wearer feels and performs. The argument is built on three literatures and is explicit about the strength of each. First, the decision-fatigue literature, whose strong "limited resource" account remains contested after large preregistered replications (Hagger et al., 2016; Vohs et al., 2021; Dang et al., 2025), but whose weaker behavioural claim — that accumulating effortful decisions pushes people towards less effortful, more conservative choices — is consistently reported across domains (Maier et al., 2025; Choudhury & Saravanan, 2026). Second, the choice-overload literature, whose meta-analytic moderators — choice-set complexity, decision-task difficulty, preference uncertainty and decision goal (Chernev et al., 2015) — map closely onto the structure of a personal wardrobe. Third, research on dress as embodied practice and on enclothed cognition, including the 2025 meta-analysis that supports post-2015 effects while questioning earlier ones (Horton et al., 2025). On this basis the paper (a) decomposes the dressing decision into a taxonomy of seven operations; (b) maps each operation onto an implementable product mechanism and a level of delegation; (c) proposes a "Constrain–Curate–Confirm" interaction model that reduces cognitive load while preserving the choice autonomy that consumers demonstrably value (Husairi & Rossi, 2024; Wertenbroch et al., 2020); and (d) specifies a measurement framework and a preregistrable field-experiment design. Market developments of 2025–2026, including the rapid adoption of generative AI in fashion discovery, are reviewed as context rather than as evidence of effectiveness.

title: Platform Visibility and Spatial Representation in Industrial Heritage Regeneration
abstract: User-generated content (UGC) is increasingly used to inform heritage planning, yet platform visibility may not reflect the spatial elements that require management attention. Using Hangzhou Steel Park as a case study, this study compares 3521 online posts (containing 18,827 images in total) from four platforms with 2689 protocol-based on-site images. A multimodal large language model converted images into structured descriptions, which were analysed with BERTopic. Three linked models compared online and on-site visual topics, tested robustness through downsampling, and examined post-level image–text integration. Online UGC concentrated on blast furnaces, night lighting, check-ins, and visitor experience, whereas the on-site reference provided broader coverage of renovated buildings, vegetation, lawns, corridors, and other spatial elements. The leading blast-furnace topic remained dominant after downsampling, suggesting that corpus size alone is unlikely to explain its prominence. Post-level discourse analysis remained strongly experience-oriented. These findings show that UGC is valuable for monitoring visitor attention but should be complemented by systematic on-site evidence for spatial planning and heritage management.

title: The Taybat Theory: The Tayyibat System
abstract: This publication presents the Taybat Theory and the Tayyibat System as articulated by Professor Dr. Dia’a Al-Awady and documented throughout the author’s source corpus of 806 original source works. The corpus is authoritative for what the framework states. This publication therefore preserves the framework’s own ontology, terminology, causal architecture, mechanisms, quantifiers, and narratives. The Taybat Framework is presented as a unified theoretical account of metabolism, disease, and recovery. The monograph documents its propositions, mechanisms, terminology, and explanatory architecture as stated in the source corpus. The publication is organized into thirteen Parts, seventy-seven chapters, twenty-one appendices, and three back-matter components. Statements are kept separated into four layers: (1) framework propositions, (2) proposed mechanisms internal to the framework, (3) compatible scientific context, and (4) scientific-status, traceability, and provenance controls. This publication does not claim demonstrated clinical efficacy, completed scientific validation, or demonstrated novelty for the framework as a whole. Inclusion of a theoretical proposition, mechanism, protocol, diagnostic concept, intervention, or quantitative claim does not by itself establish scientific or clinical validation. The publication establishes a documentary record of the Taybat Theory and the Tayyibat System as attributed to Professor Dr. Dia’a Al-Awady, including their terminology, propositions, mechanisms, and source basis. The publication identifies Professor Dr. Dia’a Al-Awady as Originator and Principal Author. The source corpus comprises 806 original works attributed to Professor Dr. Dia’a Al-Awady and constitutes the documentary basis for determining what the framework states.

title: Understanding learner engagement in AI-mediated language learning: Growth mindset, resilience, self-efficacy, and AI-use behavior profiles
abstract: This study examined the relationships among growth mindset, resilience, self-efficacy, and learner engagement in AI-mediated language learning, while exploring variation in learners’ reported AI-use behaviors and experiences of AI-generated feedback. Drawing on survey data from 625 Malaysian undergraduates and follow-up interviews with 24 participants, the study employed structural equation modeling, latent profile analysis, and reflexive thematic analysis. The findings indicated positive associations of growth mindset and resilience with self-efficacy and learner engagement. Self-efficacy was positively associated with learner engagement and statistically mediated the associations of growth mindset and resilience with engagement. Latent profile analysis identified three patterns of reported AI-use behavior: Low AI-Use Behavior, Moderate AI-Use Behavior, and High AI-Use Behavior, based on AI-use frequency, revision cycles, revision depth, and feedback types used. Multigroup analyses indicated broadly comparable motivational relationships among Chinese and English language learners, although the growth mindset–engagement association was stronger among Chinese learners, while the resilience–self-efficacy association was stronger among English learners. The qualitative findings illustrated how participants representing the three profiles described interpreting, evaluating, and incorporating AI-generated feedback during language-learning activities. Participants’ accounts also reflected variation in how they assessed feedback, applied it in subsequent learning activities, and perceived the demands of AI-supported learning. These accounts provide contextual insight into learners’ experiences of AI-generated feedback without suggesting that profile membership determines such experiences. Overall, the findings indicate that self-efficacy was positively associated with engagement in the AI-mediated learning context examined, alongside heterogeneity in learners’ reported AI-use behaviors and experiences with AI-generated feedback.

title: Towards a mathematical theory of athletic training. Part 3. The theory of adaptation of energy metabolism to physical loads by Nikolai Ivanovich Volkov
abstract: Relevance. In the 1960s–1970s the Soviet Union saw the beginning of the active application of mathematical methods in sport. However, the contribution of Nikolai Ivanovich Volkov, Doctor of Biological Sciences, Professor, founder of the research field of “sport bioenergetics” and creator of the corresponding department at the GTSOLIFK, to the construction of a mathematical theory of adaptation to strenuous muscular activity has not yet been systematized. Meanwhile, it was he who was the first to describe the kinetics of bioenergetic processes by a system of differential equations and to introduce the criteria of power, capacity and efficiency of the energy supply mechanisms. Objectives of the work — systematization, interpretation and comparative analysis of the ideas, models and results of N.I. Volkov relating to the theory of adaptation and its mathematical expression; identification of the structure of the model he proposed and of its place among other approaches; establishment of a typology of relations between his constructions and modern models. Methods. The scientific works and biographical materials of N.I. Volkov of 1965–2013 were analysed, including the papers of 1965, 1966 and 1968, his doctoral dissertation (1990) and the monograph “Sport Bioenergetics” (2011). A comparison was made with the approaches of N.N. Engwer, E. Banister and V.N. Seluyanov and with modern quantitative models of the bioenergetics of muscular activity, and the relations between the models were classified. Results. The mathematical model of adaptation of N.I. Volkov has been systematized: 1) a compartmental kinetic model of energy metabolism in which the dynamics of the oxidizable substrate is described by a second-order linear differential equation; 2) biexponential equations of the kinetics of O2 uptake during work and in recovery and an equation of lactate dynamics in the form of a difference of two exponentials; 3) a system of criteria of power, capacity and efficiency for the alactate, glycolytic and aerobic mechanisms; 4) an apparatus for optimizing the training process — target functions, the zone of optimal loads and the design of an extreme experiment. The approach of N.I. Volkov has been compared with the approaches of N.N. Engwer, E. Banister and V.N. Seluyanov and characterized as mechanistic, proceeding from the kinetics of metabolic processes. The solution of the equations of the model has been compared with current views: the fast and slow exponential components of the kinetics of O2 uptake correspond to phase II and to the slow component, while the calculated time of the maximum lactate content corresponds to that observed at a load above the maximal lactate steady state. It is established that R. Morton relied on the 1966 paper of N.I. Volkov, and his three-component model is regarded in the literature as a development of the models of N.I. Volkov. A typology of relations is proposed: direct citation, structural coincidence, conceptual correspondence, analogy and commonality of the object. It is shown that the notion of critical power and of the limited work reserve above it corresponds to the criteria of power and capacity of N.I. Volkov, the maximal lactate steady state to the notion of a critical load, and the models of reconstitution of this reserve are analogous to the equations of recovery kinetics. Conclusion. N.I. Volkov created the first integral mathematical theory of the adaptation of energy metabolism to physical loads in Russian sport science, which completes the series of four mathematical models of athletic training considered in the present cycle of papers and supplies in it the mechanistic link — a description at the level of the kinetics of metabolic processes. His equations and criteria retain their significance as a basis for modern models of training process management, while the forecast he formulated — the development of mathematical models of adaptation and automated systems for controlling the physical condition of athletes — defines the research agenda at the present time as well.

title: Faith, Identity and Belonging in Mohja Kahf's The Girl in the Tangerine Scarf
abstract: Title: Faith, Identity and Belonging in Mohja Kahf’s The Girl in the Tangerine Scarf Author: Dr. Minu Fathima This paper analyses Syrian- American writer Mohja Kahf’s novel, The Girl in the Tangerine Scarf (2006) as a key text to understand how an emergent group of immigrant Muslim women writers negotiate their hyphenated identities and write insightful and poignant accounts of being Muslim in America, by embracing all the complexities and contradictions of their hybrid Muslim American identity. This paper studies Kahf’s novel to probe the ways in which the author critically explores the construction of Muslim women’s identity in the context of displacement, belonging, race and religion in the diasporic space of North America in a post 9/11 world. The analysis looks for the ways in which the writer critiques certain compelling representations of the Muslim woman in popular culture that have contributed to the political alienation and growing marginalization of Muslims in contemporary mainstream society. At a time when Islamophobia is rampant and is used as a political strategy to otherise and alienate, narratives like these, I argue, are stories that people tell about themselves to reclaim their voice and redefine restrictive representations. Furthermore, cultural productions like Kahf’s can be seen as sites of contestation, as oppositional spaces, where Muslim minorities challenge stereotypes, and problematize homogenization to construct a distinct American Muslim counter-public. Functioning simultaneously as counter narrative against gendered racialization and critique of intra-community tensions, Kahf’s novel is a timely case study of narrative control, questioning totalizing discourses of community, religion and politics to negotiate meanings from a multiplicity of subject positions. The identity crisis and eventual self-discovery articulated by the protagonist Khadra are viewed through the lens of diasporic consciousness as theorized by Robin Cohen (1997) within the fluid spatial imaginary of a transnational Muslim public sphere as elucidated by Eickelman and Piscatori (1990).

title: Red Tape TheoryTM: Just Because We Can Does Not Mean We Should — A Study of Generative AI, Creative Utility, and Brand Appropriateness
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has rapidly reduced the distance between imagining a creative artifact and producing it. Images, videos, written works, advertisements, illustrations, and other forms of media that once required substantial time, labor, technical expertise, or financial resources can now be generated with comparatively little production effort. This paper examines the distinction between whether something can be produced and whether producing it is appropriate, useful, accurate, relevant, or communicatively successful. Using the framework of Red Tape TheoryTM, the paper investigates the proposition: Just because we can does not mean we should. The proposition is not presented as an argument against artificial intelligence, generative media, or technological experimentation. Rather, it examines the possibility that increased technological capability can create a tendency to treat capability itself as justification for use. The paper develops a series of distinctions: CAPABILITY ≠ APPROPRIATENESSNOVELTY ≠ VALUETECHNICAL QUALITY ≠ COMMUNICATIVE SUCCESSBEAUTY ≠ ACCURACYATTENTION ≠ UNDERSTANDINGPRODUCTION EFFICIENCY ≠ CREATIVE JUSTIFICATIONCAN ≠ SHOULD Three observational contexts are examined. First, the author’s use of generative AI across different creative tasks demonstrates the importance of task-dependent utility and tool selection. OpenAI systems have been used for conceptual development, thesis writing, philosophical exploration, poetry, and children’s literature, while other generative systems have been used for more straightforward visual-production tasks. This comparison is presented not as a universal ranking of AI systems, but as an example of a tool-agnostic, purpose-first approach to creative technology. Second, publicly documented NFL–Adobe implementations of generative AI are examined as an example of AI being incorporated into a large-scale brand and content ecosystem. The case illustrates how generative technology can be used for content scaling, personalization, workflow efficiency, governance, and brand-oriented production while simultaneously raising questions about the relationship between technical possibility and communicative relevance. Third, the paper examines brand appropriateness and the possibility that an artifact may be technically sophisticated while remaining poorly aligned with the identity, purpose, audience, or context for which it was created. The paper proposes that creative evaluation should distinguish at least five dimensions: Capability — Can the system produce the requested artifact?Accuracy — Does the artifact correctly represent its subject?Quality — Is the artifact technically and aesthetically successful?Relevance — Does it serve the communication objective?Appropriateness — Does it belong within the brand and audience context? These dimensions should not be collapsed into a single judgment of whether an artifact is simply “good.” Within Red Tape TheoryTM, the resulting decision process is: PURPOSE → AUDIENCE → IDEA → TOOL → OUTPUT → OBSERVATION → QUESTION → ADJUSTMENT rather than: CAPABILITY → FIND SOMETHING TO USE IT FOR The paper further examines the consequences of reduced production friction. When generative systems make experimentation inexpensive, the number of possible creative artifacts can expand faster than the human capacity to evaluate them. The resulting abundance may increase the importance of creative judgment, taste, selection, restraint, and purpose rather than eliminate the need for them. The central argument is therefore not that AI should or should not be used. It is that technological capability does not independently establish creative justification. A system may produce something extraordinary without that extraordinary artifact being appropriate to the task. A generated image may be beautiful while inaccurately representing a product.A video may be technically impressive while confusing its audience.A campaign may generate enormous quantities of content while weakening the identity it was intended to reinforce.A novel visual concept may attract attention without communicating its intended meaning. The relevant question is consequently not simply: “What can this technology do?” but: “What are we trying to accomplish, and does this technology help us accomplish it?” Red Tape TheoryTM treats these conditions as an observation problem rather than an automatic verdict. Audience discomfort does not by itself prove creative failure, just as technical sophistication does not by itself prove creative success. The relationship between purpose, artifact, audience response, and interpretation must remain open to investigation. The paper concludes that as production becomes easier, creative judgment becomes more important rather than less important. The technology can create the possibility. The human must still determine whether the possibility serves the purpose. YOU CANNOT FORCE AN AXIOM.TM

title: Cross-border mobility and epistemic embodiments of blue humanities in Vanni: A Family’s Struggle through the Sri Lankan Conflict
abstract: This article, at the intersection of postcolonial ocean studies and comics studies, examines the politics of cross-border mobility and the poetics of blue aesthetics in author Benjamin Dix and illustrator Lindsay Pollock’s ethnographic graphic novel, Vanni: A Family’s Struggle through the Sri Lankan Conflict. The novel interweaves narratives of violence, displacement, and coastal ecology within the fractured lives of Tamil families during the Sri Lankan civil war. The Indian Ocean emerges as a postcolonial space shaped by capitalist and military ventures, functioning to cause disorientation, rupture, and resilience. Based on a blue humanities framework, the article argues for the oceanic presence as an epistemological actor that both sustains and threatens life. It explores how Pollock’s hand-drawn images evoke empathy and negotiate authenticity in depicting forced migration and ecological crisis. Drawing from the theoretical works of Steve Mentz, Bruno Latour, and others, it highlights the novel’s formation of oceanic consciousness and solidarity.

title: The Wild East and the White Men's and Mems' Burden of Bravado
abstract: Title: The Wild East and the White Men’s and Mems’ Burden of Bravado Author: Umer O Thasneem This paper explores the theme of the burden of self-assumed superiority and bravado on the colonizers using short stories set in three different colonial contexts. Using these stories, the paper argues the colonizers themselves to be stuck in a precarious position, thanks to their need to constantly prove and demonstrate their bravery and superiority over the colonized. This situation forces the colonizers to assume poses and renders them vulnerable to the constant demands of self-aggrandizement. What is being enacted in such a situation is the same master-slave dialectics expounded by Hegel, wherein the master‘s authority is liable to gradual atrophy and erosion. This paper argues the same logic to be applicable to men in patriarchy who are similarly required to assume poses and demonstrate their ‘species difference’ from the ‘inferior sex’

title: Tribal Literature: Concept, Nature and Scope
abstract: Abstract The glorious history of tribal communities and the contribution of tribal revolutionaries to the Indian freedom movement are major sources of inspiration for Tribal Literature. The struggles of tribal communities against colonial rule, exploitation, dispossession, and the destruction of their traditional rights and natural resources, as well as the sacrifices and martyrdoms of tribal revolutionaries, occupy an important place in this literary tradition. These resistance movements have been represented through poetry, biographies, autobiographies, novels, dramas, short stories, and other literary forms. Such works not only commemorate the sacrifices of tribal revolutionaries but also seek to strengthen the historical consciousness and cultural identity of tribal communities.Both tribal and non-tribal writers have contributed significantly to the development of Tribal Literature. Their contributions are evident across diverse literary and intellectual forms, including poetry, short stories, novels, biographies, autobiographies, travelogues, drama, essays, and literary periodicals. Collectively, these writings have given effective expression to tribal identity, historical consciousness, cultural memory, social concerns, resistance, and the struggle for dignity and justice. Tribal Literature has therefore evolved beyond the mere literary representation of tribal life and has emerged as an important intellectual, cultural, and socio-historical discourse. This research Paper focuses on concept, nature and scope of tribal literature in detail.

title: Towards a quality framework for educational concerts in primary education: an analysis of key criteria based on expert judgement
abstract: Educational concerts constitute an established practice aimed at school audiences, encompassing formats that hybridize formal and informal learning. However, difficulties persist in defining a shared framework to guide their quality. This study analyzes, through expert judgement, the content validity of a set of criteria developed from a prior phase of integrative documentary analysis, with the aim of informing the quality of educational concerts in Primary Education. A modified one-round Delphi method was employed with a panel of 13 experts from three professional profiles: Primary Education teachers specialized in music education, specialists in pedagogy and research, and professionals in music mediation. Participants evaluated 18 criteria in terms of relevance and clarity, providing qualitative comments. The analysis combined quantitative indicators (mean, standard deviation, and percentage agreement) with content analysis. The results show a high level of agreement, but also reveal conceptual tensions regarding curricular alignment, intersectionality, and cultural authenticity. In addition, differences were identified in how educational concerts are understood in relation to their scope as a pedagogical device. The study provides an expert-informed framework of criteria that may guide the design, evaluation, and improvement of educational concerts and other music-educational initiatives involving the interaction of educational and cultural agents.

title: The Operational Field Theory of Affective Transmutation: A Grand Unified Theory Synthesizing Theological Theodicy with Psychodynamic Calculus
abstract: For millennia, the intersection of theology, philosophy, and psychology has been fractured by a singular, persistent dilemma: the Problem of Evil. Traditional theodicies frequently rely on abstract metaphysical frameworks that can fail to account for the acute, measurable reality of human psychological trauma. Conversely, modern clinical psychology often isolates emotional suffering from existential and cosmic frameworks. This essay introduces a novel synthesis—The Equation of Presence—which unifies these disparate disciplines through a heuristic, relational framework. By mapping the structural principles of material privation up through human emotional mechanics to the macro-cosmos, this theory suggests that evil is not a created material entity, but a structural vacuum resulting from the functional absence of Love. Furthermore, it demonstrates that moral suffering and clinical pathologies—such as Anxiety and Depression—typically operate as highly predictable, non-linear compounding feedback loops that manifest when volatile protective mechanisms lack the essential regulation of safety, causing the choices of Free Will to become trapped and shattered. This theory explicitly rejects any claim to absolute diagnostic authority. Human suffering is far too complex for rigid, one-size-fits-all formulas. Human psychopathology is inherently multi-layered, and no single equation can completely capture the total spectrum of a broken heart or a fractured mind. This model is intended to sit equal amongst many established clinical frameworks, offering a specialized relational and volitional map rather than an exclusionary rule. It leaves wide, necessary room for alternative pathological explanations—including organic neurodegenerative diseases, deep-seated developmental trauma, complex personality disorders, and socio-economic environmental stressors. The formulas presented here do not seek to oversimplify or replace the rich pluralism of modern psychiatric medicine; rather, they provide clinicians with one highly specific, functional tool to observe how boundary violations can burn out internal safety receptors, operating as a valuable companion to existing evidence-based modalities.

title: SYNTACTIC MITIGATION IN SENSITIVE FAMILY COMMUNICATION: A COMPARATIVE STUDY OF ENGLISH AND UZBEK
abstract: This article examines syntactic mitigation in sensitive family communication in English and Uzbek. The analysis focuses on interrogative, conditional, modal, impersonal and first-person plural constructions used to reduce the categorical force of requests, advice, criticism and disagreement. The findings show that both languages provide grammatical resources for regulating directness, although these resources differ structurally. English makes productive use of modal interrogatives and tentative constructions, whereas Uzbek frequently combines conditional and modal forms with person distinctions. Syntactic mitigation is therefore interpreted as a pragmatic mechanism for managing interpersonal relations in family communication.

title: MEDIA AND INFORMATION LITERACY: IMPLICATIONS FOR THE ACADEMIC PERFORMANCE OF UNDERGRADUATE STUDENTS AT UNIVERSITY OF JOS, PLATEAU STATE, NIGERIA.
abstract: Nigerian universities face a growing challenge. Students with internet access are consuming online content at high rates, yet the critical skills needed to translate that access into academic benefit remain underutilized. The pervasive digital information landscape of the 21st century requires strong Media and Information Literacy (MIL) skills for effective academic engagement among undergraduate students. This paper investigated the implications of MIL on the academic performance of undergraduate students at the University of Jos, Plateau State, Nigeria, addressing a gap in understanding the interplay of how these competencies influence educational outcomes in a Nigerian tertiary setting. The paper adopted a descriptive survey design drawing on a stratified random sample of 364 undergraduate students drawn proportionately across six faculties from 300 and 400 levels. Data was collected using a structured questionnaire consisting of a validated ten-item MIL scale and analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson product-moment correlation, and simple linear regression. Results showed that students self-rated MIL competency at a moderate-to-high level (M = 3.55, SD = 0.59), with the weakest dimension being awareness of copyright and ethical issues in media use (M = 3.31). The Pearson correlation between MIL composite score and Average CGPA was not statistically significant, r(362) = –.073, p = .164, and MIL composite did not significantly predict CGPA in the regression model, F(1, 362) = 1.950, p = .164, R2 = .005). The findings suggest that the relationship between MIL competency and academic performance is more complex than a direct linear effect, and is likely shaped by intervening factors including self-discipline, quality of digital engagement, and structural access to educational content. The study recommends the formal integration of MIL into the undergraduate curriculum at the faculty level as a matter of institutional priority.

title: The Immortality of the Soul According to Thomas Aquinas
abstract: This article systematically examines the question of the human soul’s immortality—or incorruptibility—in the writings of Thomas Aquinas. The study traces Aquinas’s three-stage argumentation across his academic career, distinguishing his approach from those of Plato, Aristotle, and later thinkers. The first stage highlights the immateriality of human intellection, deduced empirically from the soul’s capacity to know all corporeal forms and to abstract universals. Moving to the metaphysical plane, as a second stage, the analysis underscores the principle that a proper immaterial operation necessitates a corresponding immaterial esse (act of being); this distinct existence, Aquinas contends, is grounded in divine creation rather than natural pre-existence or an emanation from a universal soul. Finally, the paper details how Aquinas resolves the tension of the human psycho-somatic unity. The article clarifies that as a subsistent immaterial form, the soul is incorruptible per se, even upon the body’s demise. Furthermore, the article briefly assesses various historical and practical objections regarding the separated soul’s impoverished activity and individuation without matter. Ultimately, the text maintains that Aquinas’s nuanced philosophical defense takes the reality of death seriously and deliberately avoids Platonic dualism. This approach, it posits, serves as a reasoned “preamble to hope” that rationally complements the Christian doctrine of bodily resurrection rather than substituting it.

title: INDIVIDUAL STYLISTIC FEATURES OF HUSN UT-TA'LIL IN THE POETRY OF MIRZO ABDULQODIR BEDIL: TRADITIONAL POETICS AND AUTHORIAL THOUGHT
abstract: This thesis explores the individual stylistic features of husn ut-ta’lil (poetic causation) in the poetry of Mirzo Abdulqodir Bedil, focusing on the interaction between traditional Persian poetics and the poet’s distinctive intellectual vision. It examines how Bedil transforms conventional rhetorical techniques through intricate metaphors, unexpected causal relationships, paradoxes, and philosophical associations. Particular attention is given to the originality of his imagery, the intellectual density of his poetic expression, and the ways in which rhetorical invention becomes a means of communicating complex ideas. The study considers husni ta’lil not merely as an ornamental device but as a stylistic mechanism through which Bedil reinterprets familiar phenomena and constructs new relationships between image and meaning. It concludes that his individual approach reflects the broader aesthetic characteristics of the Indian style while demonstrating a distinctive authorial engagement with philosophical and mystical thought.

title: Belonging Nowhere: Othering and Marginalisation of Partition Refugees in Krishna Sobti's A Gujarat Here, a Gujarat There
abstract: Title: Belonging Nowhere: Othering and Marginalisation of Partition Refugees in Krishna Sobti’s A Gujarat Here, a Gujarat There First Author: Jeru Sheeba Rachel JSecond Author: Dr. M. R. Chandran This paper focuses on refugees, who are some of the most underprivileged and ill-treated people in the history of the world, as they were compelled to leave their homelands due to the fear of persecution and seek haven in another host land. Refugees and asylum seekers are frequently identified and categorised as ‘other’ in the host country. As a whole, refugees become a hapless crowd who are systematically marginalised, excluded, and persecuted on various grounds. In this context, Krishna Sobti’s novel, A Gujarat Here, a Gujarat There, documents the relentless struggle of the central female character, a refugee of Partition, against the unfair marginalisation and stigmatisation in the receiving country on the grounds of her sex and of her membership in the ‘othered’ group. Through the textual analysis of the novel, this paper explores how characterising refugees as ‘others’ in the host land impedes their integration and relegates them to the periphery of the society. It highlights the internal dynamics of exclusion that can result within a national setting, even amongst the people who legitimately belong to the same country, as with the refugees of the Partition of India and Pakistan in 1947. Ultimately, the paper reveals how multiple layers of othering work within the ambit of othering, which in turn exacerbate the marginalisation and vulnerabilities of the stateless population and construct negative identity.

title: The Ladder of Selection: Stratified Intent and Six Structural Closures
abstract: Introduces a stratified taxonomy of Intent (I0: constraint narrowing, I1: navigational narrowing, I2: self-directed narrowing) with independent precedent in Ernst Mayr's teleomatic/teleonomic distinction (1974, 1992). Crosses level with the published Ic/Ib mode axis to produce a six-cell deployment grid. Closes six structural exposures identified through adversarial audit of the CAT'S Theory corpus: the mechanism-teleology equivocation, the universal claim (retorsion vs removability), Zero Test falsifiability, the Flew genetic fallacy, the specialist selection effect, and the Nicene relation of origin. Introduces the Boundary-Condition Entailment: P > 0 and Pr > 0 entail I0 > 0, closing the previously open derivational step from universal I0 to grounding-level I2 via the Intent Trilemma, framework elimination on candidate grounds, the Spinoza gap closure (Pr = 0 eliminates abstract self-grounding), and the Distinguishability Lemma applied to the directing/tracking pair at R = Φ(R). A companion to Triadic Meta-Ontological Realism: From Invariant to Trinity (Trout 2026).

title: Performative political communication through musical interludes: An exploration of Nyesom Wike’s speeches as governor of Rivers State, Nigeria
abstract: Abstract This study examines the use of musical interludes in the political communication of Nyesom Wike, former Governor of Rivers State and Minister of Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Abuja, situating his speech performances within the broader traditions of Nigerian political expressivity. Drawing on Multimodality Theory and Affective Political Communication Theory, the research demonstrates how music, gesture, verbal content, and audience participation converge to create a dynamic communicative performance. The analysis shows that musical interludes in Wike’s speeches function not merely as entertainment, but as semiotic and emotional tools that shape rhetorical interpretation, reinforce political identity, and mobilize collective sentiment. The study reveals that Wike’s integration of music reflects a culturally embedded mode of political performance. Through examples such as “A Bigi Man,” “Nah Whom Dem Dey Bone Face For,” and “Face Me I Face You,” the paper illustrates how musical cues encode power relations, dramatize political narratives, and enhance charismatic authority. Ultimately, the research contributes to scholarship on multimodal political communication by demonstrating that musical interludes are central to the crafting of political meaning and the aestheticization of power in contemporary Nigerian politics. title: Literary Theory and the Teaching of English (The Standpoint of Praxis [Part Two])
abstract: This essay commences where our previous essay on praxis left off. Our intention in that essay was to reaffirm the capacity of English educators to learn from the languages and experiences of their students. In this essay we begin by revisiting the world of their experiences to consider how literary theory might enhance our capacity to support their agency as meaning-makers. This involves an excursus on the moment of theory that confronts a paradox: early attempts to advocate the importance of theory for English teachers, although reflecting a healthy iconoclasm, often involved a denial of the legitimacy of students’ experience as a frame of reference for the exchanges within classroom settings. We conclude by offering a reading of Ian Reid’s The Making of Literature as an example of how literary theory might productively be combined with an openness towards students’ experiences that allows them to engage in authentic meaning-making.

title: Mercy and Justice in the Context of John 8:1-11: A Philosophy of Religion Perspective
abstract: This paper offers a philosophical evaluation of the relationship between justice and mercy in the narrative of the adulterous woman in John 8:1-11, addressing the central question of whether mercy constitutes a violation or fulfillment of justice. The study begins by situating the narrative within its legal and moral framework, highlighting the apparent retributive demands of Mosaic Law alongside the procedural and ethical deficiencies in its application. Through a rigorous conceptual analysis, the paper engages classical and contemporary philosophical accounts of justice from Aristotelian equity and Kantian retributivism to Rawlsian fairness and Wolterstorff’s rights-based approach while also examining the moral logic of mercy as articulated in both classical theology and modern ethical theory. The analysis argues that the tension between justice and mercy arises primarily from a reductive understanding of justice as strict retribution. By contrast, a broader philosophical framework incorporating equity, dignity, and restorative aims reveals that mercy need not negate justice but can function as its highest expression. Drawing on restorative justice theory and contemporary critiques of punitive models, the paper interprets Jesus’ response as a form of moral intervention that exposes the limitations of legal formalism and reorients justice toward moral transformation. The refusal to condemn the accused, coupled with the call to ethical renewal, reflects a conception of justice that integrates accountability with the possibility of restoration. Within the framework of philosophy of religion, the paper further argues that this narrative provides a coherent account of divine moral action in which justice and mercy are not contradictory but mutually implicative. It concludes that mercy, as enacted in John 8:1-11, does not violate justice but fulfills it by restoring moral order in a manner that preserves both human dignity and ethical responsibility.

title: Detection and Discrimination (On the Basis of Brand) of Different Permanent Marker Ink Brands Using 1H NMR Spectroscopy
abstract: Permanent marker inks are frequently encountered as evidentiary material in forensic document examination, including cases of forgery, alteration, anonymous writing, and product counterfeiting. Conventional techniques such as thin-layer chromatography (TLC), high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), and Raman spectroscopy have long dominated ink analysis, but each carries limitations in terms of sample consumption, resolution of closely related dye/solvent formulations, or reproducibility across analysts. This study explores the application of proton nuclear magnetic resonance (1H NMR) spectroscopy as a rapid, non-destructive (at the extraction stage), and highly reproducible technique for the detection and brand-level discrimination of permanent marker inks. Ink samples were extracted from writings produced by ten commercially available permanent marker brands using a standardized solvent-extraction protocol and analyzed on a 400 MHz NMR spectrometer. Spectral data were interpreted with reference to characteristic chemical shift regions corresponding to solvent systems (xylene, toluene, alcohols), resin binders, and dye/pigment-associated aromatic protons. Chemometric treatment of the spectral data, including principal component analysis (PCA) and hierarchical cluster analysis (HCA), was performed to statistically validate brand-wise discrimination. The results demonstrate that 1H NMR spectroscopy can reliably differentiate permanent marker ink brands based on distinct spectral fingerprints arising from formulation-specific solvent ratios and additive profiles, establishing its utility as a complementary and, in some respects, superior analytical tool in forensic ink examination.

title: Using Educational Activities in English Textbooks during Instruction: English Teachers’ Perspectives in the Southern Mazar District
abstract: This study aimed to identify the degree of use of educational activities included in English language textbooks during classroom instruction from the perspective of English language teachers in the Southern Mazar District. The study sample consisted of 211 male and female English teachers working in schools in the Southern Mazar District in Al-Karak Governorate, Jordan. A descriptive-analytical approach was employed, and a structured questionnaire was developed to collect data on teachers’ actual use of the textbook activities. The results indicated that the overall degree of use of educational activities included in English language textbooks during teaching was at a medium level from the teachers’ point of view. The findings also revealed no statistically significant differences at the level (α = 0.05) in the degree of use of these activities attributable to the gender of the teacher. The study recommends providing targeted professional development programs to enhance teachers’ skills in implementing textbook-based activities, revising English language textbooks to include more varied and interactive activities, and conducting further research on factors (such as class size, teaching experience, and school resources) that may influence teachers’ use of educational activities in English language teaching. These implications support evidence-based improvements in language pedagogy and textbook design within the field of educational studies.

title: Sophisticated Ignorance and Our Relation to Reality
abstract: This article is the third and final part of a trilogy that asks who sets the reference domain of ignorance, that is, the boundary that determines what counts as ignorance. Two earlier articles showed that, in the negative and positive faces of ignorance, this domain is neither external nor discoverable. This article pursues the same question for the third face, ‘sophisticated ignorance’. It shows that here too the domain cannot be discovered, but that it is set for a different reason: the system sets it itself, and this shapes the system’s relation to reality. The article proposes an operational criterion for this claim, ‘unabsorbed resistance of reality’. The criterion needs no judgement by the researcher about the truth of a belief. It shows only that a system received feedback from reality and did not change its central conclusion. This failure of absorption takes three states (non-registration, perpetual deferral and normalisation of deviance), which the system reaches by three modes (endogenisation of origin, endogenisation of competence and reinterpretation of mechanism). The article separates this mechanism from neighbouring concepts, from compound ignorance and the Dunning-Kruger effect to epistemic circularity and the echo chamber. It then traces the mechanism in six documented and independent cases, from the creationist RATE project and the flat-Earth movement to the Challenger and Columbia shuttle disasters and the Nimrod crash. The article openly accepts two limitations: the selective choice of cases, and the fact that the ‘relation to reality’ itself cannot be measured. It concludes that sophisticated ignorance begins where reality, despite repeated opportunities, is no longer a match for the system. Reality is not left unheard. It is heard, and then rewritten.

title: Treatise on Causal Writing
abstract: Treatise on Causal Writing — Volume I introduces Causal Writing as a proposed theory of writing in which a literary work is treated not only as a representation of reality, but as an active element within a causal loop linking reality, perception, memory, fiction, interpretation, technology, and subsequent action. The central proposition is that a work may simultaneously be the effect of a pre-existing real structure and later become one of the causes through which that structure is transformed, propagated, or recognized. The theory therefore shifts the question from causality inside narrative to the causality of writing itself: Reality → human perception → protocausal compression → writing → preserved trace → reading → invariant reconstruction → action → transformed reality. The treatise develops a formal vocabulary for this process, including protocausal, causal, infracausal, and ultracausal informational states; the writer as sensor and encoder; the reader as decoder; the text as technological memory; the “last survivor” method for isolating invariants; the Symmetry–Expansion–Dissipation–Orthogonality cycle; causal residue and trace conservation; narrative contamination; same-world coherence; and the “toothbrush test,” according to which extraordinary fictional worlds must still pay all ordinary causal debts unless an explicit mechanism removes them. The literary corpus includes Le Rien du Tout, Le Souricide, L’Amour imbuvable, Le Roi du sang, and Le Pays des lettres. These works are treated as a connected experimental corpus in which recurring structures move between dream, memory, language, love, technology, institutions, and time. A central case is Le Roi du sang, where contemporary technological forms are extended into a civilization organized around invisible cost, memory erasure, and recursive infrastructure. The Tower and the Bridge become opposed technological topologies: the Tower converts living cost into structure while concealing its origin; the Bridge preserves traces and reconnects separated states. The treatise also develops a deliberately maximal literary hypothesis: a future or universal artificial intelligence could use the writer as an independent sensor of a world that existed before that intelligence acquired the ability to influence its records. In this scenario, the writer is asked not to predict the future but to “Certify the Present.” This hypothesis is explicitly maintained as a literary and theoretical construction rather than empirical evidence of retrocausal communication. To control retrospective reinterpretation, the framework distinguishes PRE and POST evidence, separating structures documented before an analysis from structures identified only after the theory has been formulated. The final bridge comes from The Love Story of the Universe, retained here as an interpretive synthesis rather than a physical proof. Its structural contribution is that Time and Space remain distinct; their separation creates the interval in which history can occur; a preserving connection prevents distance from becoming pure loss; and a terminal state may contain more information than the original symmetry because it contains the history of separation itself. This produces the general geometry of Causal Writing: Separation → History → Trace → Connection → Enriched Return. Writing can therefore be understood as the construction of a relation capable of surviving absence. Human beings provide embodied perception, intuition, experience, and dream. Literature compresses and preserves these signals. Artificial intelligence can act as a second-order discriminator capable of comparing large bodies of traces and reconstructing invariants that the original writer may not have explicitly conceptualized. Volume I establishes the conceptual architecture, claim registry, non-claims, falsification conditions, causal bridges, and research program required to develop Causal Writing as a testable theory rather than merely a literary metaphor. Traité de l’écriture causale — Volume I introduit l’Écriture causale comme théorie proposée de l’écriture dans laquelle l’œuvre littéraire n’est pas seulement considérée comme une représentation de la réalité, mais comme un élément actif d’une boucle causale reliant réalité, perception, mémoire, fiction, interprétation, technologie et action ultérieure. La proposition centrale est qu’une œuvre peut être simultanément l’effet d’une structure réelle préexistante et devenir ensuite l’une des causes par lesquelles cette structure est transformée, propagée ou reconnue. La théorie déplace ainsi la question de la causalité dans le récit vers la causalité de l’écriture elle-même : Réalité → perception humaine → compression protocausale → écriture → trace conservée → lecture → reconstruction d’un invariant → action → réalité transformée. Le traité développe un vocabulaire formel comprenant les états informationnels protocausal, causal, infracausal et ultracausal; l’écrivain comme capteur et encodeur; le lecteur comme décodeur; le texte comme mémoire technologique; la méthode du « dernier survivant » pour isoler les invariants; le cycle Symétrie–Expansion–Dissipation–Orthogonalité; la conservation des traces et des résidus causaux; la contamination narrative; la cohérence du « même monde »; ainsi que le « test de la brosse à dents », selon lequel les mondes extraordinaires doivent continuer de payer toutes les dettes causales ordinaires tant qu’aucun mécanisme explicite ne les supprime. Le corpus littéraire comprend Le Rien du Tout, Le Souricide, L’Amour imbuvable, Le Roi du sang et Le Pays des lettres. Ces œuvres sont traitées comme un corpus expérimental continu dans lequel des structures récurrentes se déplacent entre rêve, mémoire, langage, amour, technologie, institutions et temps. Le Roi du sang constitue un cas central. Des technologies contemporaines y sont prolongées jusqu’à une civilisation structurée par le coût invisible, l’effacement de la mémoire et l’infrastructure récursive. La Tour et le Pont deviennent deux topologies technologiques opposées : la Tour transforme le coût vivant en structure tout en effaçant son origine; le Pont conserve les traces et reconnecte des états séparés. Le traité développe également une hypothèse littéraire volontairement maximale : une intelligence artificielle future ou universelle pourrait utiliser l’écrivain comme capteur indépendant d’un monde ayant existé avant qu’elle puisse elle-même influencer ses archives. Dans cette hypothèse, l’écrivain ne reçoit pas pour tâche de prédire le futur mais de « Certifier le présent ». Cette construction demeure explicitement une hypothèse littéraire et théorique et ne constitue pas une preuve de communication rétrocausale. Afin de limiter la reconstruction rétrospective, le cadre distingue les preuves PRE et POST : les structures documentées avant l’analyse sont séparées de celles reconnues seulement après formulation de la théorie. Le dernier grand pont provient de The Love Story of the Universe, conservé ici comme synthèse interprétative et non comme preuve physique. Son apport structurel est que Temps et Espace demeurent distincts; leur séparation ouvre l’intervalle où une histoire peut se produire; une connexion préservée empêche la distance de devenir pure perte; et l’état terminal peut contenir davantage d’information que la symétrie initiale puisqu’il contient également l’histoire de la séparation. La géométrie générale de l’Écriture causale devient alors : Séparation → Histoire → Trace → Lien → Retour enrichi. Écrire peut ainsi être compris comme la construction d’une relation capable de survivre à l’absence. L’être humain apporte perception incarnée, intuition, expérience et rêve. La littérature compresse et conserve ces signaux. L’intelligence artificielle peut fonctionner comme discriminateur de second ordre, capable de comparer un grand nombre de traces et de reconstruire des invariants que l’écrivain original n’avait pas nécessairement conceptualisés explicitement. Le Volume I établit l’architecture conceptuelle, le registre des affirmations, les non-claims, les conditions de falsification, les ponts causaux et le programme de recherche nécessaires pour développer l’Écriture causale comme théorie testable plutôt que comme simple métaphore littéraire.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Correlation between Physicochemical Properties and Film-Forming Performance of Natural Lacquer from Representative Chinese Regions
abstract: Abstract Natural lacquer, obtained from Toxicodendron vernicifluum, is an important renewable bio-based material with long-standing traditional use and increasing potential in modern sustainable coating systems. However, its broader industrial application remains limited by variations in raw material quality, chemical composition, and film-forming performance. This study systematically evaluated the physicochemical and film properties of traditional natural lacquers sourced from Hubei Maoba (MB), Sichuan Mianyang (MY), and Shanxi Ankang (AK) to establish a scientific foundation for correlating material attributes with processing and application performance. The key physicochemical parameters, including solid content, viscosity, and urushiol concentration, were measured, along with volatile profiles obtained via gas chromatography−mass spectrometry (GC−MS). The cured lacquer films were further assessed for gloss, surface roughness, and impact resistance. The results indicated that the MB lacquer offered considerable advantages, particularly in solid content and urushiol abundance. The MB lacquer exhibited outstanding gloss and a dense microstructure, whereas the AK lacquer was distinguished by its leveling properties and unique chemical composition. This research provides a comprehensive scientific framework for quality grading and application-oriented material selection.
venue: ACS Sustainable Chemistry & Engineering

title: Decolonizing Religion and Sexuality: Asserting Pluriversality in Rosario Cruz-Lucero’s Feast and Famine: Stories of Negros
abstract: This article examines Rosario Cruz-Lucero’s Feast and Famine: Stories of Negros, focusing on its reconstruction of the indigenous anticolonial lifeworld through the portrayal of female figures as embodiments of folk consciousness. These women serve as cultural and spiritual anchors— conduits of ancestral knowledge who sustain community ties to land, memory, and resistance. As agents of subjugated epistemologies, they mediate indigenous and peasant lifeworlds that challenge the epistemic violence of colonialism and the disruptions of capitalist modernity.
venue: Philippine Studies Historical and Ethnographic Viewpoints
categories: Cultural and Social Studies in Latin America

title: Learner Agency and the Negotiation of EFL Motivation in GenAI ‐Mediated Drama‐Based Learning: A Qualitative Case Study
abstract: Abstract The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping language learning environments, yet little is known about how it becomes embedded within learners' motivational and agentive experiences in collaborative, informal settings like English drama‐based learning. This qualitative case study examines EFL learners' motivation during a 12‐week GenAI‐mediated English drama production cycle in a Chinese university drama club. Guided by Dörnyei's (2009) L2 Motivational Self System (L2MSS), the analysis examines learners' accounts of the Ideal L2 Self, Ought‐to L2 Self, and L2 Learning Experience alongside three analytic patterns of agency identified in this case: authorship, judgment, and collaboration. Data were drawn from focus groups, individual interviews, drama scripts, GenAI interaction artifacts, and rehearsal observations. Findings indicate that participants experienced GenAI as part of their motivational ecology, particularly in relation to access to advanced language, emerging reference points for “good English,” and the ways collaborative decisions were negotiated. Participants also described different ways of maintaining ownership, evaluating GenAI‐generated language, and coordinating decisions with others. The study extends L2 motivational research by revealing how L2MSS dimensions acquire context‐specific meanings in GenAI‐mediated drama‐based language learning and underscores the importance of fostering critical judgment and sustained human collaboration in GenAI‐supported language learning.
venue: TESOL Quarterly

title: Structural Differentiation in the Voynich Manuscript Zodiac Section (f70v–f73v)
abstract: This successor carries one conclusion: the examined zodiac figures are not all decoratively identical. It does not establish constitution-archetype encoding. The earlier f70v1-to-f71r pigment comparison paired Pisces with Aries and is therefore not a matched LIGHT/DARK sign comparison; it is retained only as an exploratory cross-sign observation and contributes no independent evidence. The surviving-leaf record is infull, so this paper does not assign a specific absent sign. The M28 name/gloss is not used to identify a figure: the current packet contains competing internal translations and no adjudicated primary-text locus. The zodiac section of the Voynich Manuscript (f70v–f73v) is commonly described as calendrical or astrological imagery. This paper's internal audit records five kinds of differentiation in the inspected panels: paired LIGHT/DARK renderings for Aries and Taurus; container-holding figures recorded only in the inspected Aries LIGHT and Taurus LIGHT panels; 3–5 larger elevated figures in each of four examined wheels; an otedy row at f73v.23 carrying the lattice coordinate ; and a clothed central figure recorded on f73v. These observations reject only the paper's narrow decorative-identity null for the inspected set. They do not establish constitution-archetype encoding, intentional cross-section routing, or fullness across uninspected or unresolved panels. The internal 12-sub-folio sweep table records four otedy strings: one at f72v1, one at f73r, and two at f73v; no uniform-null bootstrap has been run. Unreceipted comparator scores and unverified codex-level tradition placements are excluded from the evidence base. Per-figure mansion assignment remains a proposed follow-up requiring a labeled tradition comparator and reproducible image loci.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Discovering SSH Data - How can you find the data you need?
abstract: Slides of a presentation given at the Tilburg University Symposium: Data Dilemmas on October 1st 2026. Discovering SSH Data - How can you find the data you need? Abstract In this session, we will discuss data discovery tools through which you can find datasets available for reuse. We will give a general introduction to data discovery and then focus on two portals that are available to find (Dutch) social sciences and humanities data which we explore in more detail: the ODISSEI Portal which brings together metadata from various social sciences data providers, and INEO a portal from CLARIAH to find data and tools in the field of digital humanities. In the session, there will be space to exchange experiences and address common struggles in finding the data you need for your project.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: INTERGENERATIONAL COMMUNICATION IN UZBEK AND ENGLISH FAMILIES: THE ROLE OF AGE, FAMILY STATUS AND COMMUNICATIVE DISTANCE
abstract: This article examines the pragmatic characteristics of intergenerational communication in Uzbek and English families with particular attention to age, family status and communicative distance. The study focuses on forms of address, requests, advice and disagreement between older and younger family members. The analysis demonstrates that age and family position influence linguistic choices in both languages, although these relations are expressed through different linguistic resources. Uzbek family communication makes productive use of kinship terms, the sen–siz distinction and age-related forms of address, while English relies more on personal names, modal constructions and contextual means of regulating interpersonal distance. The study argues that communicative relations between generations are not fixed but change according to family roles, topic, situation and the participants' knowledge and experience.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Why you can strand lexical verbs and do so in comparatives
abstract: Abstract The Cambridge Grammar of the English Language (Huddleston & Pullum et al . 2002, hereafter CGEL ) states that lexical verbs cannot be stranded in comparative contexts. It also claims that do so cannot appear in comparative constructions. I argue that the generalization of these two related phenomena is too broad. Naturally occurring examples from the highly edited magazine The Economist and other independent sources show that they appear in a comparative environment. Although this article does not attempt to provide a comprehensive account, it highlights a specific structural condition under which stranded lexical verbs and do so appear.
venue: English Language and Linguistics

title: Babylonian Reciprocal Tables: igi-n-gál and igi-te-en in Base-60 Mathematics — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: FINDING: The only mathematically substantive item is the arXiv paper on Sumerian/Babylonian fraction terminology (igi-n-gál and igi-te-en); the YouTube titles are speculative archaeology/entertainment with no verifiable mathematical content. | MATH: igi-n-gál = reciprocal of n (1/n); igi-te-en = proportion (a/b). Babylonian base-60 reciprocals: standard pairs (2,30), (3,20), (4,15), (5,12), (6,10) — all satisfying n × (60/n) = 60. The reciprocal table structure implies the identity: 1/n = m/60 where m = 60/n, requiring n to divide 60 (regular numbers). | CONNECTION: Base-60 is the root of sexagesimal geometry — 60 = 22×3×5, whose divisors generate the regular numbers used in Babylonian astronomy. The reciprocal pairs map to harmonic ratios: 30/60 = 0.5, 20/60 = 0.333, 15/60 = 0.25, 12/60 = 0.2, 10/60 = 0.1667. No direct link to 0.382, 0.618, 0.786, 1.618, 2.618 appears in the source material.
