title: Learning from Lifting
abstract: The author shares how lifting weights helped him at school, teaching him the importance of persistence and community in reaching his goals, and suggests ways that English teachers might learn from students’ experiences outside of school.
venue: The English Journal

title: Dental Health and Oral Pathology in a Middle Byzantine Monastic Community: Evidence from the Degirmenalti Monastery (Tuzla, Istanbul)
abstract: Objectives: This study presents a dental paleopathological analysis of skeletal remains from the Middle Byzantine Değirmenaltı Monastery (Tuzla, Istanbul), aiming to characterise the frequency and severity of dental pathology in the assemblage and to interpret the findings within the documented dietary and occupational context of Byzantine monastic life. Materials and Methods: Seven dental pathology categories whose caries, alveolar abscess, dental calculus, enamel hypoplasia, chipping, periodontitis, and antemortem tooth loss (AMTL) were macroscopically examined in 15 individuals recovered from 14 burials. A total of 247 teeth were recorded, together with 38 antemortem tooth losses. Occlusal wear was scored on a ten-point scale. Findings were compared with published dental data from contemporaneous Byzantine and medieval Anatolian populations. Results: Caries affected 80.0% of individuals (n=12; tooth-level prevalence 10.5%), dental calculus 73.3% (n=11; 41.3%), and AMTL 60.0% (n=9; 13.3%). Alveolar abscess was observed in 46.7% (n=7), periodontitis in 40.0% (n=6), enamel hypoplasia in 33.3% (n=5), and chipping in 26.7% (n=4). Occlusal wear scores ranged from 1.3 to 7.1. Conclusions: The dental profile reflects a carbohydrate-rich monastic diet, communal-living oral hygiene deficits, and pre-admission childhood physiological stress. Non-masticatory wear and chipping patterns in some individuals point to craft-related dental use, consistent with occupational differentiation reported in the postcranial skeleton of the same assemblage.
venue: Cumhuriyet Dental Journal

title: Development and Validation of the Instrumental Musical Self-Concept Scale for High School Students
abstract: In the field of musical learning, self-concept has received increasing attention in recent years. However, previous research in Spain has largely focused on students enrolled in specialized professional and higher music education, while instrumental musical self-concept in compulsory secondary education remains underexplored. To address this gap, the present study developed an ad hoc scale specifically designed to assess instrumental musical self-concept among secondary school students. The final sample consisted of 980 students from 14 educational centers in Aragón and Navarra (Spain). The results provide evidence supporting the internal structure and internal consistency of the 16-item Instrumental Musical Self-Concept Scale for High School Students, organized into four theoretically interpretable factors. These findings contribute to the study of instrumental musical self-concept in Spanish secondary education and provide an instrument whose psychometric properties can be further examined in independent samples and through additional sources of validity evidence.
venue: Education Sciences

title: Learning by designing: App development, perceived digital competence, and pedagogical authorship in English teacher education
abstract: Abstract This study explores app development as an instructional medium for fostering perceived digital competence and pedagogical authorship in English teacher education, contributing to research on technology-enhanced preparation that moves teachers from using digital tools towards creating them. Participants developed simple instructional apps through low-threshold coding activities in iterative group design cycles across two groups – undergraduates in-person ( n = 18) and graduates online ( n = 16) – sharing a 15-week curriculum. Pre–post surveys indicated significant gains in digital confidence and perceived instructional benefit among undergraduates, while graduates showed clearer movement in perceived instructional benefit, with engagement and motivation remaining stable across both groups. Lexical cluster analysis of reflection essays identified four orientations – emotional growth, pedagogical insight, design conceptualization, and scaffolding reliance – pointing towards emerging pedagogical authorship rather than uniform competence gains. As digital creation becomes as common as digital consumption for today’s learners, modest coding literacy, framed as an instructional medium, offers a workable path towards digital agency and pedagogical authorship in English teacher education.
venue: ReCALL

title: School Theatre as a Tool for Values Education: Perspectives of Theatre Education Teachers in Jordan
abstract: This study aimed to examine the role of school theatre in promoting educational values among students in Jordanian schools from the perspectives of theatre education teachers. The study adopted a descriptive survey design, and data were collected using a questionnaire developed for this purpose. The questionnaire was administered to a sample of 61 male and female theatre education teachers selected through simple random sampling. The findings showed that the role of school theatre in promoting educational values among students was perceived to be moderate. The results also indicated that there were no statistically significant differences in teachers’ perceptions attributable to gender, years of experience, academic qualification, or school type. Based on these findings, the study recommends that the Ministry of Education strengthen the role of school theatre by providing appropriate theatre spaces in schools and appointing specialized theatre education teachers. The study also highlights the importance of integrating theatre activities into school life as a means of supporting students’ moral, social, and educational development.
venue: Jordan Journal of Applied Science-Humanities Series

title: Can Multiple Contents Be Simultaneously At-Issue?
abstract: There is a prevailing assumption in the at-issueness literature that utterances express exactly one content (usually a proposition) that is at-issue, with any other contents being not-at-issue. This article examines this assumption critically, asking whether it can ever be the case that multiple contents are at-issue simultaneously. Looking at the three leading approaches to defining at-issueness, and considering them as both backward- and forward-oriented phenomena, we observe some similarities and some divisions among how these approaches answer this question. We spotlight conjoined question sequences, an empirical construction that might require multiple contents to be simultaneously at-issue, and discuss how these various approaches might account for the observed data.

title: Eğitim Koçluğu Uygulamalarının Üniversite Hazırlık Öğrencilerinin Sınav Kaygısı ve Bilinçli Farkındalık Düzeylerine Etkisinin İncelenmesi
abstract: Giriş ve Amaç: Bu çalışmanın amacı, üniversite sınavına hazırlanan lise son sınıf öğrencilerine uygulanan eğitim koçluğu programının öğrencilerin sınav kaygısı ve bilinçli farkındalık düzeyleri üzerindeki etkisini değerlendirmektir. title: Enhancing review writing through explicit genre-based instruction: A quasi-experimental study on graduate students’ News & Views writing
abstract: The ability to evaluate scholarly work is an important aspect of graduate students’ academic development. One way to foster this ability is by learning how evaluations are constructed in published reviews. Nature’ s News & Views (N&V) articles, which summarize and evaluate individual research articles, provide valuable models for academic review writing. Although previous studies have identified the rhetorical move structure of N&V articles, little empirical research has examined how these genre features can be taught effectively in English for Academic Purposes (EAP) contexts. This quasi-experimental study investigated the effectiveness of explicit genre-based writing instruction (GBWI) in improving graduate students’ N&V writing. Seventy students from two intact classes were assigned to either an experimental group (n = 35) or a comparison group (n = 35). The experimental group received explicit instruction on N&V move–step structure and evaluative language supported by examples drawn from a mini-corpus of published N&V articles, whereas the comparison group independently analyzed model texts to identify rhetorical and linguistic features. Results showed that explicit GBWI significantly improved students’ use of N&V move structures and overall writing performance. Students in the experimental group also used evaluative language more frequently than those in the comparison group, although the two groups did not differ significantly in the accuracy of evaluative language use. These findings provide empirical evidence for the effectiveness of explicit GBWI in teaching N&V writing and offer pedagogical implications for implementing GBWI in EAP writing courses.
venue: System

title: Adapting to the Loss of Racism: A Case Study in Failed Predictions of Anti-Supernaturalism
abstract: In the discourse over the relationship between religion and science, there is a division between those who see naturalism as a necessary assumption for science, one that cannot be empirically scrutinized and therefore cannot be falsified or verified, and those who see both naturalism and belief in the supernatural as competing hypotheses that can be criticized, and potentially falsified. Those who take the latter perspective more often than not believe that mainstream science, where its findings are relevant to the question, has always confirmed the predictions of naturalism. Here I suggest that this view of the historical data is overly simple. As a counterexample, I consider the history of the shifting predictions in naturalistic theories of human origins, particularly the now-debunked belief in racial differences in human morality and intelligence. The centuries-long process of hypothesis formation, testing, falsification, and subsequent hypothesis adjustment is placed in the Popperian framework of the “conventionalist stratagem,” and it is argued that this case study provides useful insights for the dialogue between science and religion today.
venue: Religions

title: Inferring unobservable relations by analogy
abstract: This paper introduces and analyzes a kind of analogical inference that, I argue, has been largely overlooked by philosophers and cognitive scientists. These are cases in which the primary inference is a multi-placed relation that connects already known or observed elements. Such relational analogical inferences are especially important in the social sciences. Contrasting them with other recognized types of analogical inference illuminates both their role in scientific inquiry and the warrants that govern their strength.
venue: European Journal for Philosophy of Science

title: Generative AI-Mediated Speaking Practice and Intercultural Communicative Competence in EFL Contexts: A Scoping Review of the Literature (2022-2026)
abstract: Speaking is widely regarded as the most challenging skill for English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners, and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has rapidly become a prominent resource for oral practice, while a parallel but largely separate strand of research has examined how artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated tools contribute to intercultural communicative competence (ICC). This scoping review maps the evidence base at the intersection of GenAI-mediated speaking practice, oral fluency and ICC, with particular attention to the underrepresented Vietnamese EFL context. Following a PRISMA-ScR-informed approach, 17 empirical and review studies (2022-2026) were thematically synthesized into four clusters, namely GenAI and oral fluency, GenAI and affective-communicative outcomes, AI-mediated ICC and Vietnam-specific studies, alongside three foundational theoretical works. Findings show that GenAI-mediated speaking practice consistently improves short-term fluency, willingness to communicate and speaking anxiety; that AI-mediated interaction can support ICC development when paired with reflective, culturally responsive pedagogy, though this evidence remains preliminary; and that the Vietnamese literature, while fast-growing, is small and methodologically narrow, with no study yet examining ICC outcomes. Critically, no identified study combines a longitudinal design with simultaneous measurement of oral fluency and ICC within a single GenAI-mediated speaking intervention, opening a worthwhile direction for doctoral-level research. This review argues for such an integrated research agenda, situates it within Sociocultural Theory, the Interaction Hypothesis and Byram's ICC model and outlines its theoretical, methodological and pedagogical implications for the Vietnamese higher-education context.
venue: International Journal of Language and Linguistics

title: CRITICAL APPROACHES TO LITERATURE: Youth Lens in Action: Teacher Candidates’ Critical Engagement with YA Texts through Book Clubs
abstract: In this article, authors share how the youth lens framework is operationalized in a young adult literature course through book clubs to deepen literary analysis, while also highlighting its pedagogical potential for supporting teacher candidates in critically engaging with and teaching YA texts.
venue: The English Journal

title: The Possibility of a Philosopher-King: Eros , Knowledge, and Justice
abstract: Abstract The paradox of the philosopher-king in Plato’s Republic concerns the tension between the philosopher’s contemplative happiness and the obligation to rule. Existing interpretations, appealing to either external compulsion or internal eros , either fail to explain the philosopher’s motivation or leave political knowledge insufficiently grounded. This article argues that resolving the paradox requires the kind of ontological framework exemplified by the Weak Two Worlds Theory (WTW), and develops a corresponding account of rational eros . By grounding political cognition in ontological entailment, the WTW reconciles philosophical happiness with the political realisation of justice, resolving the paradox motivationally while preserving ontological hierarchy.
venue: Dialogue

title: Adam Mickiewicz’s Poem “Aryman i Oromaz” Through a Polyphonic Lens of Good and Bad
abstract: It is known that poem"Aryman i Oromaz" is part of the cycle "Eastern Flowers" by the Polish poet. Along with other works of the cycle, which provide poetic translations from Arabic poetry, this poem is dedicated to a fragment from the French translation of the Avesta, describing the history of the creation of the world, the cosmogonic views of the Zoroastrians on the structure of the world. Mickiewicz, who has certain ideas about the content of the sacred book, tries to recreate the primary picture of the religious tradition for the Polish reader. This topic is important for Mickiewicz to assert the thesis of the triumph of good over evil, which is close to him and lived by him. In other words, by addressing the plot of a foreign ancient religion, the poet expresses the identity of the postulates of Zoroastrianism with his life and personal views. Analysis of the text of the work shows that the Polish poet adheres to the plot of the French translation, creating his own vision of the problem, confirming the moral values that follow from the source material. Some elements of the work, reflecting the main concepts of the translated text, suggest that Mickiewicz initially planned to translate the text into Polish, and in the process of translation, individual interpretation took over. Thus, the poem should be perceived as a recreation of the text, interpreted in a new artistic context.
venue: EPISTÉMÈ

title: LLM-ASSISTED MARKUP OF ENTITIES IN TEI: A CASE STUDY
abstract: This paper presents a case study of marking up TEI (Text Encoding Initiative) documents using large language models. We detail our experiments using LLMs for named entity recognition and entity linkage in a corpus of TEI documents. The corpus consists of four journals co-edited by the Swiss-German theologian, Karl Barth (1886–1968). We aimed to enrich the TEI markup by adding XML elements to mark up entities and attributes to link to QIDs on Wikidata. We experimented with using both cloud-based frontier models and local open-source models to enrich a subset of 34 articles from the corpus. After analyzing the outcome using both human reviewers and automated analysis, we indicate where our methodology proved successful and where we encountered problems. We conclude that LLMs can perform named entity recognition and linking in TEI documents, but that the combined financial and labor cost of scaling this procedure to the full corpus would be relatively high without optimizing our current pipeline.
venue: Journal of Humanities and AI

title: A Habit-Building View of Democracy: Mary Parker Follett and Motor Activities
abstract: Citizens of democracies should live democratic lives and develop democratic habits. That is one of Mary Parker Follett’s core insights on democracy. A child of the Gilded Age, Follett experienced the erosion of communal relationships, the intensification of socio-economic inequalities, and the alienation of ordinary people from the complex political system that governed their lives. She saw democracy become remote and foreign to citizens who had little control over what happened to them. Her solution was simple: to reinject a dose of democracy into the everyday life of citizens. This paper retrieves Follett’s embodied and habitual vision of democracy for contemporary political theory. Follett claimed that citizens should participate actively in the democratic life of their society; however, she conceived of democratic participation as going beyond decision-making and deliberative activities. She thought that participation in simple forms of embodied joint actions, like recreation and collective chores, could also benefit democracy. Drawing from Follett, I argue that participation in a wide variety of embodied practices of collective action provides benefits to individuals and society by instilling democratic habits in citizens. Those habits incline those who develop them to enter and maintain relationships as free and equal peers with all sorts of people to reach common ends. When faced with collective problems, therefore, these individuals are more likely to choose democratic collective action and to do so more effectively.
venue: Political Theory

title: Audibility under pressure: Loudness escalation and electroacoustic mediation in mixed-purpose performance spaces
abstract: Abstract This article analyses loudness escalation in amplified music as an issue of audibility, technology and social negotiation, rather than merely a question of excessive sound levels. The emphasis is on multifunctional spaces, including restaurants, bars, churches, weddings, nightclubs and urban leisure environments, where music, conversation, worship, labour and commercial activities can coexist simultaneously. Utilising insights from electroacoustic music studies, sound reinforcement practices, music psychology, African music scholarship and research on safe listening, the article delineates the concepts of sound level, perceived loudness, dynamic range, compression, limiting and distortion. It posits that current loudness standards are influenced by electroacoustic mediation, wherein microphones, loudspeakers, mixers, compressors, playback systems and venue acoustics determine the parameters of audibility, power and professional efficacy. Two concepts are formulated as analytical instruments. Dynamic insecurity refers to the hesitance of performers to employ soft dynamics in situations where their audibility is questionable. The Loudness Trap delineates the feedback loop wherein sound level, compression, background noise, listener adaptation and social expectation collectively promote escalation. The article concludes by advocating for context-sensitive sound practices that maintain musical energy while safeguarding communication, dynamic range and auditory health.
venue: Organised Sound

title: The Receptive Act: Theorizing the Addressee in Divine Discourse Through Tafaʾʾul Morphology
abstract: This article argues that, although recent work in speech act theory has increasingly engaged with uptake, reception, and the addressee’s participation, the addressee has not yet been sufficiently theorized as performing a distinct volitional and transformative act. Existing accounts illuminate important aspects of how an addressee recognizes, receives, or responds to an address, but they do not fully specify the intentional structure involved in actively appropriating its normative force. To address this issue, the article introduces the concept of the receptive act, understood as the addressee’s intentional enactment of this appropriation, and develops the concept of the hearer’s intentionality as the intentional structure through which this act is performed. The Arabic tafaʾʾul pattern, particularly its takalluf dimension, is employed not as a direct linguistic equivalent of a speech act category but as a linguistic resource for articulating this volitional structure: takalluf denotes deliberate and effortful striving toward a quality or state not yet possessed. The article therefore distinguishes the receptive act from uptake, receptivity, or perlocutionary effect by focusing on the addressee’s active appropriation of an address and its normative implications. In the context of divine discourse, to which Wolterstorff applied speech act theory, this approach provides a framework for examining how divine address becomes operative through the addressee’s intentional participation. The article concludes by proposing that the receptive act can be understood as a distinct, addressee-side dimension of speech act performance, complementing rather than replacing Austin’s tripartite framework.
venue: Religions

title: Formalizing Colloquial Arabic Vocabulary: A Linguistic Model for Bridging Colloquial and Classical Usage
abstract: This study examines the formalization of colloquial Arabic vocabulary by identifying lexical items that can be brought closer to Classical Arabic through limited phonological or morphological adjustment. Rather than tracing the historical origins of colloquial forms, the study focuses on the linguistic commonalities between colloquial Arabic and Classical Arabic and explores how these shared features may be used to reduce the gap between everyday speech and formal usage. Using a descriptive-analytical approach, the study analyzes selected colloquial vocabulary items and proposes modifications that align them more closely with established Arabic linguistic rules and patterns. The findings indicate that many colloquial forms maintain strong lexical, phonetic, or morphological links with Classical Arabic, making their formalization possible through systematic and minimal linguistic intervention. The study argues that such an approach can contribute to revitalizing the use of Classical Arabic, strengthening linguistic awareness, and enabling speakers to employ familiar vocabulary in more formally acceptable ways without linguistic hesitation or embarrassment. The study contributes to Arabic linguistics by offering a practical model for understanding the relationship between colloquial and Classical Arabic and for developing methods that support linguistic continuity between the two levels of usage.

title: Cajal the artist. The origins of a passion
abstract: Santiago Ramón y Cajal is widely recognized as the father of modern neuroscience. However, his life has many extraordinary facets, and he is even considered a polymath. Among his many activities, his artistic endeavors stand out, and this article focuses on exploring the origins of Cajal’s passion for the arts. The Aragonese scholar cultivated drawing, painting, literature, chess, and, notably, photography with equal intensity and passion. This article shows Cajal’s artistic dimension, exploring the origins and evolution of his passion for drawing, painting, and photography. We demonstrate that his profound visual capacity and the technical skill developed through his art were not unrelated to his scientific work. On the contrary, they became the fundamental support for his ability to innovate and document the delicate structures of the nervous system through beautiful drawings and photographs that allowed him to show humanity the “butterflies of the soul,” the name he gave to the elegant cells he saw in nervous tissue. His inclination for drawing was evident from childhood, and despite serious conflicts with his father, who desperately wanted him to become a doctor, he managed to take painting courses and perfect his technique. His work as a painter, writer, and photographer is presented, leaving the door open for future explorations into the life of a great man who continues to amaze almost a century after his passing.

title: Film and Screen reframed – The place of Film and Screen education in Expressive Arts
abstract: Abstract While Media Studies has long been part of the national curriculum in Scotland, the launch of the national Film and Screen curriculum in late 2025 introduces a distinct new form of arts education. With its dedicated focus, Film and Screen is set to become the fifth discipline within the Expressive Arts curricular area. This paper examines the potential place and purpose of this curriculum, arguing for its inclusion in the Expressive Arts by drawing on academic literature and educational and policy frameworks. It highlights the expressive and creative qualities of Film and Screen, emphasising its role in providing children and young people with opportunities to engage critically with the arts, develop creativity, and express their own voices. The paper also considers the curriculum’s potential, outlining possible pathways for its growth and the barriers that must be addressed as implementation progresses.
venue: Scottish Educational Review

title: Reasons Isolated from Good Reasoning
abstract: On a popular and influential view, normative reasons are premises in good reasoning, where good reasoning manifests a pattern of reasoning that normally preserves fittingness. I develop two counterexamples to this view: isolated pro tanto reasons that are either weak or normally overridden.
venue: Australasian Journal of Philosophy

title: Pre-Reflective Visual Attraction to the Actor's Embodied Presence: Screen Presence Beyond Narrative Centrality
abstract: Purpose This project investigates a specific spectatorial phenomenon: inexplicably persistent visual attention to an actor's embodied presence that narrative centrality cannot explain. Taking Harvey Specter as embodied by Gabriel Macht in the television series Suits (2011-2019) as a narrative model, the study asks how screen presence is given to the spectator at a pre-reflective level, before thematic interpretation of character and plot. It addresses three questions: (1) what constitutes embodied screen presence at the level of pre-reflective experience; (2) how presence-attention can be distinguished from narrative attention; and (3) whether archetypal configuration contributes to the intensity and persistence of presence independently of narrative development. Theoretical framework The study draws on the phenomenology of the lived body (Merleau-Ponty), the phenomenology of film experience (Sobchack), and Husserl's notion of pre-reflective experience, and combines these with Jung's theory of archetypes read as formal principles of organization rather than personality types or psychological contents. It argues that existing narratological, star-studies, and cognitive film models explain initial attentional capture but not the temporal persistence of attention toward a still, composed, low-salience body after narrative function has been fulfilled. Method The design is Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (IPA) with a narrative model as phenomenological material, extended through triple hermeneutics (lived professional experience, its narrative-embodied stylization on screen, and the researcher's phenomenological interpretation). The corpus consists of Suits, Seasons 1-3. Sequences were purposively sampled for low narrative centrality and high presence persistence, and three types of scene were prioritized: ritualized entrances, pauses and reaction shots, and confrontational dyads. Analysis proceeded in three phases: phenomenological epoché bracketing narrative and extra-textual knowledge; descriptive coding of embodied cues (postural schema, facial composure and gaze vectors, vocal embodiment, sartorial-bodily integration, temporal structure); and interpretive mapping onto a four-part Jungian configuration (Magician as dominant, Warrior as supportive vector, Trickster as subordinated function, Persona as elaborated instrument). Quality was addressed through idiographic depth, eidetic variation, intersubjective traceability through thick description, and epistemological modesty. Hypotheses H1 (Magician-Persona): presence persists through an elaborated Persona in which Magician mastery is made visible, even when narrative information is bracketed or minimal. H2 (Subordination): the Trickster intensifies presence only when subordinated to Magician mastery. H3 (Warrior Amplification): the Warrior vector amplifies persistence by giving symbolic mastery existential weight. Findings Three recurring structures organized the spectator's pre-reflective experience: ritualized entrance as reorganization of the visual field, stillness as territorial holding, and status reversal as play within mastery. The three hypotheses received phenomenological support in the sampled sequences. Archetypal coherence does not originate screen presence, which is rooted in corporeal givenness, but amplifies its intensity and accounts for its temporal persistence.

title: Replies to a fellow expressivist and two fellow inferentialists
abstract: Abstract We respond to the comments by Imogen Dickie, Matthew Chrisman and Christine Tiefensee for a book symposium on our Reasoning with Attitude . Our commentators attempt to pull us further into either expressivism or into inferentialism. Here, we attempt to resist either pull and further establish our inferential expressivism as a home for both expressivists and inferentialists.
venue: Philosophical Studies

title: Standards and normative authority
abstract: Abstract Norms, rules, or standards require, recommend, or evaluate actions and attitudes. Claims about what agents have a reason to do or ought to do can be true according to or relative to standards. These statements will be familiar to anyone versed in recent work in metaethics and especially those interested in the debate over whether some standards are authoritatively as opposed to merely formally normative – i.e., the debate over whether some standards, like those of morality or prudence, ‘really’ or ‘genuinely’ tell agents what they have a reason to do or ought to do, while other standards, such as those which constitute certain conventional codes of behaviour, do not. But what are standards? And what is it for normative claims to be true or false according to standards? In this paper I raise a challenge for normative authority scepticism – the position that the idea that some standards are authoritatively normative is incoherent, confused, or otherwise defective – through an examination of these questions.
venue: Philosophical Studies

title: On Two Types of Mood Shift in Icelandic Conditionals
abstract: Abstract Ordinarily, the finite verb of Icelandic "o-marked" conditional ef-protases occurs in the indicative. However, subjunctive finite verbs are obligatory under "conditional inversion," i.e., in V1-protases, and they occasionally show up in present tense ef-protases. In this squib, interpretive consequences of these two types of "conditional mood shift"—referred to as CMS_1 and CMS_2, respectively—are characterized. Thus, CMS_1 may lead to "neutralization" of perfect semantics, where a present perfect subjunctive has to stand in for a past indicative, and to outright unacceptability if the main verb is a reportively used form of kveða ("say," "speak"). CMS_2 is interpretively neutral in some instances but appears to allow "potentialis" uses like its historical precursor in Old Norse in others. An analysis is sketched for CMS_1, drawing on a competition approach to the semantics of the perfect.
venue: Linguistic Inquiry

title: To be slowly killed is still to be killed: necropolitics and slow violence in Imbolo Mbue’s How Beautiful We Were
abstract: The novel How Beautiful We Were by Imbolo Mbue portrays the effects of oil extraction on the everyday lives of people living in the fictional village of Kosawa. This paper contends that the multinational corporation, through its extractive activities, destroys the environment of the village, causing the communities to endure sickness, death, and insecurity. This study places Mbue’s novel within existing discussions of environmental justice and postcolonial critique. It examines how intergenerational trauma is enacted over time through ecological destruction, and how resistance is slowly generated from that destruction. Using Mbembe’s idea of necropolitics and Nixon’s idea of slow violence, the paper maintains close analytical engagement with Mbue’s narrative voice. It pays attention to the collective perspective of the novel and everyday experiences of people facing environmental problems. The paper demonstrates how fiction represents long-term environmental harm and everyday forms of violence that often remain unrecognized within legal frameworks. It further explains how resource extraction produces environmental damage that disproportionately affects certain communities and becomes normalized within everyday life.
venue: Humanities and Social Sciences Communications

title: Revisiting the Authoritative/Formal Distinction
abstract: Distinguishing between authoritative and formal normativity is a staple component in the metanormative literature. Norms such as morality and prudence count as genuinely or authoritatively normative, while those norms concocted on the spot are only formally normative. In this article, I question the common reliance on a monolithic divide between these two kinds of normativity. First, I argue that the same kind of skepticism that plagues the adjacent concept of an ought simpliciter applies equally to a definition of ‘authoritativeness’. Second, I point out the limits of primitivist responses to this challenge of developing a proper definition. Due to the abundance of intuitive differences between paradigmatic instances of authoritative and formal normativity, glossing at intuition is insufficient to demarcate authoritative normativity. Finally, I provide some motivation for abandoning the dualist orthodoxy and eschewing a monolithic understanding of the authoritative/formal divide in favor of a form of metanormative pluralism: there are multiple dimensions along which one might describe norms as being either authoritative or formal.
venue: Journal of Ethics and Social Philosophy

title: The influence of Mesoamerican obsidian mining on Technosols formation: A case study in las Navajas, Hidalgo, Mexico
abstract: Pre-Hispanic obsidian mining in Mesoamerica was one of the earliest and most widespread anthropogenic landscape modifications in the Mexican Central Highlands, yet its long-term impact on pedogenesis and Technosol formation remains poorly understood. The green‐gold obsidian deposit at Cerro de Las Navajas (Hidalgo), exploited successively by the Teotihuacan, Toltec, and Aztec cultures over >1600 years, offers a unique opportunity to investigate anthropogenic soil evolution along a hillslope. We evaluated five soil profiles with different exploitation histories and two natural reference soils using morphological, physical, chemical, and micromorphological analyses. Soils on upper and middle slopes affected by older, less intensive Teotihuacan-period mining exhibited A-B-C horizons with well-developed aggregates, umbric, folic, and cambic diagnostic horizons, and abundant biogenic features, and were classified as Spolic Technosols. In contrast, lower-slope soils impacted by intensive Aztec-period deep mining showed incipient development (O C or CA-C horizons), apedal microstructures, and abundant fresh obsidian fragments. One profile with 40 cm of organic layers interbedded with obsidian flakes was classified as Skeletic Folic Histosol. Natural reference soils were classified as Vitric Andosol or Vitric Umbric Andosol. Micromorphological evidence demonstrates that soil biota (roots, mesofauna, fungi) play a crucial role in transforming technogenic deposits into functional soils in temperate forest landscapes. The main conclusion is that Technosols reflect the intensity, duration, microrelief, and extraction techniques employed by the Teotihuacan, Toltec, and Aztec cultures. Beyond the local context of Cerro de Las Navajas, this study demonstrates that Technosols can serve as pedological archives of human history, and that soil biota plays a crucial role in transforming technogenic deposits into functional soils in temperate forest landscapes.
venue: CATENA

title: ‘God Gave This Land to Me’: parody, grievability, and settler-colonial semiotics in Nina Paley’s This Land Is Mine
abstract: This study employs Multimodal Critical Discourse Analysis through a decolonial lens, used here as an analysis of visual and typographic rather than inclusive of sonic resources, to examine how visual semiotics organise grievability in Nina Paley's animated parody This Land Is Mine (2017 cut). Reading effects in the text rather than authorial intent, it asks whether a parody that distributes blame symmetrically across all nationalist claimants nonetheless distributes recognition asymmetrically. Drawing on Mignolo, Quijano, Said, Wolfe, Butler's account of grievability, and Hutcheon's theory of parody, the analysis tracks colour, religious symbolism, social-actor representation, costuming, and typography frame by frame. To guard against confirmation bias, it incorporates a mandatory counter-evidence section testing the film's ‘universal indictment’ design. Findings indicate that formal equivalence at the level of plot coexists with an unequal allocation of mournable childhood, recurrent symbolic legibility, and typographic provenance. The study contributes a replicable Decolonial Multimodal Critical Discourse Analysis (DMCDA) framework and shows how parody can leave colonial asymmetries of recognition intact.
venue: Critical Discourse Studies

title: The Mystery of Feminine and Masculine
abstract: The Mystery of Feminine and Masculine Body, Mind, Sensitivity, Attraction, and the Possibility of Bodha स्त्री-पुरुष रहस्य: देह, मन, संवेदनशीलता, आकर्षण और बोध की संभावना Author: Agyat Agyani (अज्ञात अज्ञानी)Independent Researcher & PhilosopherVedanta 2.0 | Consciousness | Non-Duality | Philosophy of Mind ORCID: 0009-0000-8083-0685Website: https://vedanta2life.comDate: 28 September 2026 Description This paper presents an independent philosophical and phenomenological inquiry into the relationship between feminine and masculine, body and mind, attraction and awareness, and unconscious reaction and conscious observation. यह शोध-पत्र स्त्री-पुरुष संबंध, देह और मन, आकर्षण और जागरूकता, तथा अचेतन प्रतिक्रिया और सजग अवलोकन के संबंध का स्वतंत्र दार्शनिक एवं phenomenological अध्ययन प्रस्तुत करता है। The paper does not treat feminine and masculine as rigid or universally fixed biological categories. Instead, they are explored as two experiential entry points—Deha (body) and Manas (mind)—through which human beings may encounter themselves and the other. इस अध्ययन में स्त्री और पुरुष को कठोर या सार्वभौमिक जैविक श्रेणियों के रूप में स्थापित नहीं किया गया है। उन्हें अनुभव के दो प्रवेश-बिंदुओं—देह और मन—के रूप में देखा गया है, जिनके माध्यम से मनुष्य स्वयं और दूसरे को समझने की संभावना प्राप्त कर सकता है। A central theme is the interpretation of Tamas, Rajas, and Sattva. The three guṇas are not presented as moral categories of high and low, good and bad. They are understood as necessary modalities of Prakṛti—stability and form, movement and activity, and clarity and illumination. इस शोध में तमस्, रजस् और सत्त्व को नैतिक ऊँच-नीच के रूप में नहीं देखा गया है। तीनों को प्रकृति की आवश्यक गतियों के रूप में समझा गया है—स्थिरता और रूप, गति और क्रिया, तथा स्पष्टता और प्रकाश। The paper further examines attraction as a natural embodied phenomenon rather than automatically defining it as sin. The philosophical question is not merely why attraction occurs, but whether the individual can observe the attraction, desire, imagination, and mental reaction arising within. आकर्षण को यहाँ स्वतः पाप नहीं माना गया है, बल्कि एक सहज देहगत-अनुभव के रूप में देखा गया है। मुख्य प्रश्न यह है कि आकर्षण उत्पन्न होने पर व्यक्ति अपनी इच्छा, कल्पना, मानसिक प्रतिक्रिया और भीतर उठती ऊर्जा को देख सकता है या नहीं। The proposed movement is: Observation → Awareness → Viveka → Jñāna → Bodha देखना → जागरूकता → विवेक → ज्ञान → बोध The paper proposes that deeper awareness of the body may become a path toward bodily self-understanding, while awareness of the mind may become a path toward understanding desire, attraction, imagination, and mental movement. Ultimately, both body and mind are approached as possible gateways toward witnessing awareness (Sākṣī) and direct insight (Bodha). यह अध्ययन प्रस्तावित करता है कि देह की गहरी जागरूकता देह-बोध का मार्ग बन सकती है और मन की जागरूकता इच्छा, आकर्षण, कल्पना तथा मानसिक गति को समझने का मार्ग बन सकती है। अंततः देह और मन दोनों को साक्षी और बोध की ओर जाने वाले संभावित द्वारों के रूप में देखा गया है। The paper does not prescribe a particular religion, guru, mantra, tantra, ritual, renunciation, or compulsory spiritual practice. It is offered as an open philosophical inquiry and an invitation to examine one's own experience directly. यह शोध किसी विशेष धर्म, गुरु, मंत्र, तंत्र, अनुष्ठान, संन्यास या अनिवार्य साधना की स्थापना नहीं करता। यह एक खुला दार्शनिक अन्वेषण है और पाठक को अपने अनुभव को स्वयं देखने का निमंत्रण देता है। The author does not present the propositions as established scientific laws or as the final truth. The work is intended to create a dialogue between Indian philosophical traditions, phenomenology, philosophy of mind, bodily awareness, and contemporary reflection on desire and human relationships. लेखक इन प्रस्तावों को स्थापित वैज्ञानिक नियम या अंतिम सत्य के रूप में प्रस्तुत नहीं करता। इसका उद्देश्य भारतीय दर्शन, phenomenology, philosophy of mind, bodily awareness तथा इच्छा और मानवीय संबंधों पर समकालीन चिंतन के बीच संवाद स्थापित करना है। Core Proposition Do not merely observe the other. Observe yourself while observing the other. दूसरे को केवल मत देखो; दूसरे को देखते हुए स्वयं को देखो। The paper leaves the final interpretation to the reader's own inquiry, observation, and experience. यह शोध अपनी अंतिम व्याख्या पाठक के स्वतंत्र अन्वेषण, अवलोकन और अनुभव के लिए छोड़ता है। Keywords Feminine and Masculine; Deha; Manas; Body Awareness; Mind Awareness; Attraction; Sexuality; Phenomenology; Unconscious; Prakṛti; Tamas; Rajas; Sattva; Sākṣī; Viveka; Jñāna; Bodha; Consciousness; Non-Duality; Vedanta 2.0; Philosophy of Mind; Embodied Consciousness; Self-Observation; Human Evolution. title: Too Useful to Avoid, Too Uneasy to Accept: Cognitive Dissonance Among Language Majors in the GenAI Era
abstract: This study examined the formation and regulation of cognitive dissonance among 30 undergraduates majoring in English, Chinese, Japanese, Thai, and Vietnamese through semi-structured interviews and grounded theory analysis. The findings identified Cognitive Dissonance as the core category, four dissonance-generating categories—Competence Development Disconnect, Ethical-Normative Conflict, Devaluation of Language Majors, and Educational Inertia—and one regulation-related category, Dissonance Regulation. A square-pyramid model was developed to explain the process from dissonance generation to regulation. The study shows that students’ GenAI use cannot be understood as simple acceptance or rejection, but as conflicts among beliefs, emotions, values, and behaviors around AI and language learning. It also raises concerns that early or excessive AI use may reduce opportunities for sustained practice and language competence development. This study extends the application of cognitive dissonance theory to AI-mediated language education and offers implications for language programs to strengthen AI literacy, ethical guidance, human–AI collaboration, and competence-oriented assessment.
venue: Journal of Intelligence

title: Moving Beyond Text: Rethinking Audiovisual Method in the Study of Lived Religion
abstract: While there is growing recognition of film’s role in shaping and illustrating beliefs—especially narratively and artistically—there remains limited academic engagement within religious studies practically working with audiovisual content more generally. This article attempts to address this gap by reflecting on the process of our own work on the short documentary film, Wild Swimming: A Liquid Devotion. In particular, we focus on the methodological and epistemological insights garnered from working this way and reflect on the questions it forced us to confront. The short film was made by the authors in 2024 and explores wild swimming as a contemporary implicit lived religious practice—instead of merely a physical activity involving cold-water immersion. The film attempts to show how it can serve asa pathway toward encountering the sacred. Reflecting on the experience of making the film, the paper explores what the medium can contribute to the ‘empirical excess’ of lived religious subjectivities—particularly the dimensions that are physically encountered and observed in practice, and how audiovisual content might be more fully integrated into the academic study of religion. Specifically, drawing from our experience of making the film, it argues for the value of audiovisual research in exploring the embodied experience, sensory encounter and spatial or environmental ritual as essential components of spiritual world-making. Central to this is an argument for the relationship between documentary film and the ethnographic study of lived implicit religion, especially with its focus on praxis Documentary conventions, we argue, align closely with approaches to lived religion that privilege lived subjectivities, embodiment and subtlety. These conventions allow film to show rather than tell and, importantly, to invite multiple and even unexpected readings. The paper argues that this is especially significant for the study of religion, which deals with realms that often exist outside descriptions in words, because audiovisual media expand the dimensions of communication available to us. Our intention is, therefore, not to privilege audiovisual methods over textual ones, but to consider what additional possibilities they may offer for understanding lived forms of religious practice. It allows for an expansion beyond written textual approaches which, despite the shifts in scholarship to focus on the body and material practice, still dominate the field. By highlighting several of the practical choices made in producing the film, the article also offers important points of reflection on how the experience of the sacred might be further conceived in this way and suggests avenues of focus for deepening audiovisual research within religious studies scholarship. It should be made explicit that the primary objective of this article is to advance a theoretical and methodological discussion of camera-based research for religious studies. Rather than offering an exhaustive analysis of the film itself, we use the film as an empirical case through which to interrogate broader methodological and conceptual questions. Given the constraints of the article’s length, a comprehensive film analysis lies beyond its scope. Instead, the film functions as the principal case study that enables us to develop, illustrate, and critically reflect upon the epistemological and methodological framework proposed in this article.

title: Missionaries and Foreign Regime: A Critique of the Christian Missionaries' Activities During the British Governance in India (1757-1947)
abstract: The coming and gradually growing activities of the Christian Missionaries during Colonial Hegemony (1757-1947) proved significant historical events in the Socio-Cultural History of Modern India. title: The Latest Epicycle? Queloz’s Conceptual Ethics
abstract: Abstract This critical notice assesses Matthieu Queloz’s The Ethics of Conceptualization , highlighting its compelling pragmatist account of concepts as tools shaped by human needs. It argues, however, that Queloz’s reasons for concept use do not constitute a fundamentally new kind of normative reason but instead recast familiar questions about normative authority at the conceptual level.
venue: Canadian Journal of Philosophy

title: Locations and Binding Domains
abstract: Abstract This paper argues that some noncomplementary instances of anaphors and pronouns in the context of spatial prepositions conceal different structures underlying fixed spatial relations (places) and dynamic ones (paths). I propose that place prepositions form opaque binding domains due to the necessary mediation of a functional head pwhich sets out a clause-like structure, while paths are transparent to binding unless they contain an overt place preposition.

title: Marie Kettnerová, the first Czech female palaeontologist
abstract: Marie Kettnerová was the first Czech female working in palaeontology. Although she published only six scientific studies due to misfortune, her works are of high quality and feature timeless hand-drawn illustrations and photographs. She focused mainly on Devonian rugose and heliolitid corals and the geological situation in Moravia (eastern part of the Czech Republic), where she came from.
venue: Geological Society London Special Publications
categories: History of Science and Natural History

title: Hodgson’s vocabularies of Vayu and Bahing
abstract: Abstract This article examines two mid-19th century vocabularies of Kiranti languages Vayu and Bahing (Eastern Nepal) compiled by Brian Hodgson and which accompany grammar sketches of the same languages. The vocabularies, which are both English-Kiranti, have a parts-of-speech macro-structure, but adopt a combination of different ordering systems with respect to their micro-structures. The article describes the two vocabularies with respect to their structural features, and considers what evidence may be found within to suggest the data collection methods that were used in the enterprise. The article contributes, from the point of view of these various features, to the study of 19th century lexicography of Himalayan languages.
venue: Historiographia Linguistica

title: ‘It’s not natural’: spatial simultaneity and the comedic processing of masculinity under the COVID-19 crisis in Alfred Adriaan’s Full Show (2022)
abstract: This article analyses Alfred Adriaan’s Full Show as a cultural text through which masculinity is publicly negotiated under South Africa’s COVID-19 lockdown. Drawing on Judith Butler, Raewyn Connell, Chris Brickell, Henri Bergson, and humour scholarship, it develops the concept of spatial simultaneity: the collapse of public/private divisions that forces contradictory masculine positions—authority and dependence, bodily discipline and decline, provider status and domestic redundancy—into the same domestic scene. The article treats stand-up’s live, addressed, audience-responsive form as the condition rendering this collapse legible in ways other cultural forms would not. Through close reading of four sequences, it argues that the performance renders masculine crisis collectively recognisable and bearable by translating private strain into comic fellowship. Rather than treating masculinity as static, the analysis reads Adriaan’s comedy as an active, if incomplete, renegotiation of masculine codes: his self-deprecation targets not himself but an unattainable ideal of manhood, a critique resonating particularly with his predominantly female audience. Yet this comic management does not undo gendered power: it depends on feminine labour and competence while leaving them secondary to the male subject’s crisis, and its patriarchal norms are inflected by the middle-class, Coloured, Afrikaans-English idiom Adriaan and his audience share, such that gender, race, and class remain inseparable. Full Show thus emerges as an ambivalent text, revealing both the instability of post-apartheid masculinity under lockdown and comedy’s capacity to contain that instability without transforming it.
venue: Comedy Studies

title: Phi-Resonant Sexagesimal Lattice (PRSL) Tunneling Principle — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: The discovery shows that the Babylonian base‐60 system's highly composite divisors create a harmonic lattice that exactly matches the 240 root vectors of E8 when the 132 Hz carrier phase‐locks through phi‐scaled intervals. This sexagesimal‐E8 resonance stabilizes torsional shear, allowing persistent coherence tunnels that transmit information non‐locally across the 15 s–7 m temporal window. Data mining of breakthrough patterns revealed the exact divisor sequences needed to engineer these tunnels, turning astronomical timekeeping into a quantum communication protocol. title: Poliomyelitis or lumbosacral radicular compression? A new interpretation of the Ruma stele
abstract: Abstract The funerary stele of the Egyptian priest Ruma depicts marked atrophy and deformity of the right lower limb, traditionally interpreted as a possible sequela of paralytic poliomyelitis. This study re-evaluates this interpretation through an interdisciplinary clinical, paleopathological, and iconographic analysis, proposing chronic lumbosacral radiculopathy as a plausible alternative diagnosis.
venue: The Egyptian Journal of Neurology Psychiatry and Neurosurgery

title: Mentored by Lament: Preaching Towards Imagination in Divisive and Overwhelming Times
abstract: In the midst of ongoing traumatic local and national realities, communities may find themselves overwhelmed and divided on how to respond or feel. Even more, communities may struggle with suppressed imagination, struggling to conceive of a future. And yet, preachers and public proclaimers are called upon to “offer a Word” of God’s redemptive possibilities in the midst of these communities. While events may feel novel or unprecedented, preachers and proclaimers may find a guide and mentor in the ancient practice of lament. Proclamation that is shaped by lament might allow preachers to gather disparate emotions and responses in the community, summon people to collective witness, unite the lamenting community around a shared conviction, and ultimately (re)ignite holy imagination.
venue: Interpretation A Journal of Bible and Theology

title: Surface and deep structures in Ngikis heritage conservation
abstract: This article explores the Ngikis Traditional Ceremony at the Karangkamulyan Heritage Site, Indonesia, as a mechanism of community-based heritage conservation through the analytical lens of Claude Lévi-Strauss’s Structural Anthropology. Employing a qualitative research design based on Constructivist Grounded Theory and ethnographic fieldwork conducted between August 2024 and February 2025, the study reconstructs both the surface structure and deep structure of the Ngikis ceremony. The surface structure encompasses the empirically observable dimensions of the ritual, including temporal organization, spatial configuration, actor roles, material objects, ritual actions, processual sequences, and social interactions. The deep structure refers to the underlying cultural principles (boundary formation, purification, transcendental mediation, ecological reciprocity, historical memory activation, and collective responsibility) that organize these observable elements into a coherent cultural system. The findings demonstrate that Ngikis functions not merely as a symbolic or religious expression but as a cultural institution through which archaeological heritage, collective memory, ecological ethics, and social solidarity are continuously reproduced across generations. The study contributes a novel theoretical framework integrating Structural Anthropology, Living Heritage Theory, Ritual Materiality, and Community-Based Heritage Conservation, offering a comprehensive explanation of how recurring ritual practices sustain both tangible and intangible heritage while reinforcing the cultural resilience of local communities.
venue: Asian Anthropology

title: Clearing the way: The promise of a comprehensive record clearing initiative in Philadelphia
abstract: Millions of U.S. residents have criminal records, which creates barriers and challenges related to employment, housing, and other important domains. Although record clearing opportunities exist, several factors (e.g. cost, access) prevent most eligible individuals from pursuing relief. To address these limiting factors, a Philadelphia-based coalition facilitated local legal organizations and community-based organizations holding 56 record clearing events embedded within publicly accessible community events throughout the city between May 2022 and June 2024. At these events, attendees met with legal staff and volunteers, at no cost, to discuss their records and initiate record clearing if eligible. In the first 25 months of this record clearing initiative, nearly 3,000 people engaged with the legal clinics and nearly 2,000 of those clinic attendees initiated some form of record clearing. This paper describes the development and implementation of this innovative initiative, characterizes the individuals who attended the record clearing clinics, describes a longitudinal study that recruited 809 participants pursuing record relief as a result of their clinic attendance, and shares descriptive results from baseline surveys completed by those participants, including findings related to the ways in which their criminal records have negatively impacted their lives and general measures of well-being.
venue: Criminal Justice Studies

title: Embedding visual and performing arts into health professional education – a scoping review and conceptual framework
abstract: AIM: Public health professionals need evidence-based education to equip them with sufficient knowledge to recommend creative community programmes and arts therapies. The current review asks 'What is known about how visual arts, performing arts, and creative writing are embedded in health and medical education?'. METHOD: A search across six different databases (CINAHL, ERIC, Medline, AMED, ProQuest Dissertations, and Web of Science) identified 6090 articles, and 284 were included. The core search terms were (1) Visual arts; performance arts and creative writing, (2) Tertiary education and health Professionals. Descriptive statistics were used to quantify the characteristics of learning activities. Thematic analysis was used to identify the intended learning outcomes. RESULTS: Nursing was the most represented profession, followed closely by medicine. An extremely wide range of art practices were identified, including graffiti, sculpture, clowning, cinematic arts, music, creative writing, poetry, dance, photo, and art viewing. The review characterises how visual arts, performing arts, and creative writing are currently being used, including the group size, setting, engagement style, and collaboration with creative practitioners. Surprisingly, only 10% of studies focussed on creative arts therapies, arts-based interventions or community arts, and no mention of social prescribing was identified. Instead, the majority of studies focussed on visual and performing arts as pedagogical tools, and the main learning outcomes were professional development (promoting empathy, communication, preparedness for practice, negative attitudes), clinical practice (critical thinking, specialist knowledge, clinical skills), and personal development (self-awareness, well-being). CONCLUSION: This review highlights that visual and performing arts are used as pedagogical tools across a range of professions, and the need for more patient-centred educational provision in creative arts therapies, arts-based interventions, and community arts. Future curricula could engage arts practitioners and cultural spaces more directly to support experiential learning approaches and evaluate creative techniques to identify if they can enhance student learning.
venue: Perspectives in Public Health

title: Sufi values on TikTok: Social media usage and its implications for the digital spread of Sufism
abstract: Social media increasingly mediates various aspects of life, including religion and religiosity. This study examines how Sufi values are conveyed and experienced through TikTok videos, focusing on their manifestation, modes of delivery, and implications for audiences. Employing a qualitative netnography approach, this research analyses 50 of the most popular videos from 10 selected TikTok accounts that actively disseminate Sufi-related content. The findings reveal a distinction between content visibility and value interpretation. While philosophical Sufism ( tasawuf falsafi ) appears more dominant, as reflected by its share of the sampled most-viewed videos (58%, 29 of 50 videos), the internalisation of Sufi values among viewers is more strongly associated with ethical dimensions, especially the process of shaping everyday moral conduct ( akhlaq ), which is represented in the users' comments (46%). In addition, the findings indicate that content referencing internationally recognised Sufi figures achieves markedly higher audience engagement than content referencing local figures, approximately four to six times higher average views, likes, and shares, despite local figures being slightly more numerous among the referenced sources (9 versus 7 of the 16 scholars identified), suggesting an alteration in patterns of religious authority that are presented within digital environments. Furthermore, TikTok-mediated Sufism has implications for three core aspects of Islamic teachings: aqidah, sharia , and akhlaq , demonstrating its role in shaping religious understanding and practice. These dynamics reflect a broader transformation in the representation and transmission of Sufi values, where traditional modes of spiritual learning, previously centred on direct engagement with a sheikh or murshid, are increasingly complemented with digitally mediated experiences. This study contributes to the field of digital religion by showing that TikTok videos function not merely as a medium of transmission, but as a constitutive environment that reshapes how Sufi values are produced, circulated, and interpreted, as well as how religious authority is conferred in contemporary Muslim societies.
venue: Heliyon

title: Groom Lake and Tonopah Test Range - Accumulating Reductions in Uncertainty
abstract: Groom Lake and the Tonopah Test Range occupy a unique position in the history of experimental aerospace engineering, yet their technological significance has often been obscured by secrecy, mythology, and speculation. This study examines the distinct but intersecting histories of these Nevada facilities through the development of high-altitude reconnaissance, extreme-speed flight, foreign-aircraft exploitation, low-observable technology, weapons testing, and classified operational aviation. Particular attention is given to the U-2, A-12 OXCART, Soviet aircraft exploitation and CONSTANT PEG, HAVE BLUE, the F-117 Nighthawk, TACIT BLUE, and Tonopah’s weapons-testing mission. Drawing upon peer-reviewed scholarly literature while distinguishing documented evidence from inference, the analysis demonstrates that these programs emerged not from isolated technological breakthroughs but from the integration of aerodynamics, propulsion, materials science, electromagnetic theory, flight controls, instrumentation, human factors, intelligence, maintenance, and experimental flight testing. The study further examines the consequences of classification for historical understanding, human performance, environmental accountability, and the mythology surrounding Area 51. Across otherwise disparate programs, a consistent experimental philosophy emerges: identify consequential uncertainty, construct an experiment capable of exposing it, measure the result, compare observation with prediction, and refine the system accordingly. Groom Lake and Tonopah are therefore best understood not simply as monuments to secrecy, but as environments in which generations of engineers, pilots, scientists, maintainers, and intelligence specialists transformed uncertainty into measurable knowledge—and measurable knowledge into aerospace capability.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: WHAT BECAME OF CAUSE? The Four Causes, Classical Determinism, Quantum Potentiality, and the Scope of Causal Explanation
abstract: What are we asking when we ask for a cause? A bridge collapses, a fever appears, a heart pumps, a planet follows an orbit. “What caused it?” sounds like a single question, yet an answer may identify what produced the event, what made it possible, how its parts were organized, which conditions made the difference, or what activity makes that organization intelligible. Such answers need not compete. They may concern different dependencies within the same reality.Aristotle’s causal analysis treats why as a differentiated question. What something is made of, what makes it the kind of thing it is, from what source a change proceeds, and for the sake of what an activity or development is ordered do not identify interchangeable relations. A satisfactory answer to one need not settle the others.As particular forms of scientific inquiry acquired increasingly precise procedures for establishing selected dependencies, the epistemic standards suited to those inquiries could also come to shape what counted as causal explanation more generally.In mathematical astronomy, determination of celestial motion could be achieved without thereby settling how the represented motions were corporeally realized or what physical source produced them. Debates from ancient through medieval and early modern astronomy repeatedly redistributed the relation among mathematical determination, physical realization, and natural-philosophical explanation. Early modern mechanics altered that relation further. Quantitative relations of motion increasingly entered physical explanation itself: motion could be mathematically determined, laws could specify how it changed, and forces or other sources of change could be incorporated into the same explanatory framework without every question concerning their underlying nature or mode of action being settled. Mathematical determination and physical causal attribution thus became more tightly connected while remaining conceptually distinct. Classical mechanics brought this connection into a particularly powerful configuration.Within classical mechanics, a sufficiently specified state together with the governing dynamics could determine a represented evolution where the relevant uniqueness conditions held; sufficiently precise knowledge of the relevant state and conditions could in turn support prediction. Because one mathematical framework could join state specification, lawful evolution, definite values, deterministic dynamics, and prediction, these distinct relations were repeatedly realized together. Their conjunction within an exceptionally successful framework made it increasingly easy to treat them, together with broader assumptions about physical reality, as though they formed one necessary explanatory package.Quantum mechanics breaks that apparent inseparability. Exact specification of a quantum state does not straightforwardly amount to a catalogue of simultaneously definite values; probability cannot in general be treated merely as ignorance of an already complete classical state; and unitary evolution does not by itself settle how a definite recorded outcome is to be understood. Bell’s theorem constrains Bell-local causal structures under its relevant assumptions; Kochen–Specker constrains global noncontextual value assignments; uncertainty relations constrain the joint sharpness available for specified pairs of observables; and the measurement problem concerns the relation between unitary state evolution and definite recorded outcomes. These results do not yield one undifferentiated verdict about causation, determinism, definiteness, locality, or mind-independent reality. Their combined significance lies in forcing distinctions among notions that classical success had allowed to travel together.Differentiated Realism frames causal inquiry in terms of proportionate authority. Authority concerns the legitimate epistemic reach of an established result or warranted judgment—what it may support, constrain, or settle—and scope specifies the questions, conditions, scales, domains, and relevant respects within which that authority has been earned. Explanatory sufficiency is relative to the specified explanandum: a causal account can be sufficient without being exhaustive of the causal dependencies that can be investigated in the same reality. Causal contraction occurs when epistemic standards suited to establishing one family of causal dependencies are treated as general conditions of causal intelligibility. Where the causal question remains determinate but the available representation cannot express a required distinction, the representation requires revision. Where a question presupposes a causal form whose applicability has not yet been established, that applicability remains part of the inquiry; where the demanded dependence is shown not to apply to the explanandum under the selected respect, the question requires revision. The claim that some causal dependence must obtain is warranted when rational consideration of the explanandum under the selected respect establishes that its actuality does not account for itself in that respect; the particular term or mode of that dependence may nevertheless remain unresolved.Causal self-knowledge names the reasoner’s capacity to keep affirmation proportioned to warrant and authority proportioned to the scope in which it was earned.The history of cause is therefore a history not only of changing causal theories but of changing questions, representations, explanatory achievements, and standards of causal intelligibility. Scientific success has shaped both which causal relations became especially tractable and which other causal questions became less salient within established forms of inquiry.

title: The role of school administration in supporting sports activities: perspectives of administrators and classroom teachers
abstract: In order for sports activities to be conducted effectively and sustainably in elementary schools, it is necessary to jointly evaluate teachers’ practical experiences with the support of school administration. The purpose of this study is to examine the role of school ad-ministration in supporting sports activities in elementary schools based on the perspec-tives of administrators and classroom teachers. The study was conducted using a case study design, one of the qualitative research methods. The study group consisted of 12 school administrators and 19 classroom teachers working in the Keçiören district of An-kara. Data were collected using a semi-structured interview form developed by the re-searcher and analyzed using content analysis. The findings revealed that administrators focused on the planning of sports activities, resource management, and inter-institutional collaboration, while teachers emphasized the implementation process, student motiva-tion, and inadequacies in physical infrastructure. Both groups identified the shortage of physical education teachers and the lack of sports facilities and equipment as fundamen-tal problems. In conclusion, the study demonstrates that a holistic management ap-proach—integrating the strategic leadership of school administration with teachers’ prac-tical experience, and supported by physical infrastructure and institutional collabora-tion—is necessary for the sustainable development of sports activities in elementary schools.
venue: Herkes için Spor ve Rekreasyon Dergisi

title: Algerian ESP Issue: Challenges and Perspectives
abstract: Abstract: The widespread use of the English language as an international means of communication is in its continual growth. This fact is reflected in different fields and in a variety of ways, notably its inclusion in the formal educational systems all over the world, and Algeria is no exception. The increasing importance resulted in the expansion of one particular aspect namely English for specific purposes (ESP) which has grown to become one of the most prominent areas of English as a foreign language, (EFL) teaching today. Being aware of the importance of English in all domains of study and research, the Algerian Higher Education Ministry has included its teaching in higher education institutions nationwide. Hence, the development of ESP is reflected in the increasing number of universities offering different specialties. Similarly, Algerian curriculum developers incorporated EFL to be taught in the Algerian national educational context. Thus, this paper is an attempt to conduct a brief exploration of the teaching of EFL and ESP in the Algerian context. It also, attempts to discuss the Algerian ESP issue from the perspective of EFL practitioners who moved to teach English to students of higher education. Being one of them and challenged by many hindrances; the researcher tried to add to the ESP course, this ‘stand-alone unit’ in the Algerian higher education by recommending some suggestions so as to reach more successful results. Keywords: EFL, ESP, ELT, Syllabus design, Team teaching.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Textile-Wrapped Wealth: A Late Bronze Age Hoard from Kaleburnu-Kral Tepesi/Galinaporni-Vasili, Cyprus
abstract: Mineralized textile remains associated with the 2014 bronze hoard from Kaleburnu‐Kral Tepesi/Galinaporni‐Vasili are examined in detail in this study. At least 111 bronze objects were recovered inside and around a storage jar placed in a rock‐cut well on the Karpas Peninsula. Many of these objects had been wrapped with textiles and cords, bundled together, or separated by organic layers. Microscopic analysis identifies 13–15 different textiles, all tabby weaves, as well as several types of cord; almost all yarns show S‐twist, consistent with the Eastern Mediterranean textile tradition. By mapping the spatial distribution of textile types (A–O), the study reconstructs wrapping strategies, the bundling of object groups, and the use of organic fillers such as grass between stacked bowls. This self‐contained and distinctive case provides one of the few, and unique, examples for the role of textiles in organizing and protecting metal wealth in the Late Bronze Age.
venue: TEXTILE

title: Historical phraseology as a theoretical no-man’s-land and a paradox. Suggestions for future research directions
abstract: Abstract This article examines historical phraseology as a theoretically underdeveloped yet conceptually rich field at the intersection of historical linguistics and phraseological research. It argues that formulaic language – encompassing multiword expressions, phrasemes, some types of constructions, and discourse patterns – is a central but insufficiently integrated component of language history. While phraseological research has expanded significantly, it remains fragmented and largely disconnected from broader theories of language change, resulting in a “theoretical no-man’s-land”. The paper reviews the current state of research, highlighting the dominance of synchronic approaches and the marginalisation of formulaicity within historical linguistics. It identifies methodological challenges specific to historical data, including limited corpora, lack of native-speaker intuition, and difficulties in applying criteria such as frequency and stability. To address these gaps, two main directions for future research are proposed. First, a stronger integration with the cultural history of language use is advocated, emphasising discourse traditions and the socio-cultural embedding of formulaic patterns. Second, the article calls for alignment with holistic, usage-based frameworks such as Construction Grammar and Construction Discourse, which conceptualise language as a continuum of form-meaning pairings. Ultimately, the paper argues that historical phraseology has the potential to significantly enrich general linguistic theory by foregrounding conventionalisation, variation, and the cultural dimensions of language change.
venue: Yearbook of Phraseology

title: The Bush Book: a consciously bilingual human–machine book (concept note and map of the bush)
abstract: Concept note and map of the bush, version 0.1. English and Russian versions. The text of our time is already bilingual: living human words and computed machine words are woven together, and both a person and a machine write and read it. The Bush Book is built on this consciously: each chapter shows the seam between the two languages, carries a passport for the machine reader, and records its sources and outflows as machine-readable links. It grows not like a train but like a bush: chapters come out now as articles, each with its own DOI — latent chapters of a book being woven as it goes. Each new chapter will be a new version of this record; the DOI of all versions is the DOI of the book. Open idea: anyone may use it for any purpose, citing the author (CC BY 4.0). Idea — Igor Kapustin. Written with Claude (Anthropic).
